### Closed planar histories on the fixed graph

By Response 1, failure on a 2-computad is equivalent to a nonempty positioned history from an empty path at some vertex $x$ back to that empty path. Its first move must have empty input at $x$ and its last must have empty output there. If the component of $x$ has no internal branching, it is a singleton without a loop or a simple directed cycle. Every loop at $x$ stays in this component. In the first case either of the required moves is already a scalar. In the second, the output of a birth and the input of a death at $x$ are powers of the same cycle based at $x$. For positive exponents $m,n$, use the birth $\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)/m$ times, then the death $\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)/n$ times. A zero exponent already gives a scalar. Thus the two necessary tests at the *same vertex* suffice, even with arbitrary additional rules between different vertices. [Planar criterion](#researcher-response-1)

For hardness it suffices first to encode the one-object hard instances over two loops. Use the stack code $c_i=P(PQ)^iQ$ of round-1 Response 113. From **every** starting stack each $c_i$ emits its original edge $i$ and restores the stack. In a positioned rewrite $l\,c(u)\,r\to l\,c(v)\,r$, read $l$ from the chosen initial stack, and read $r$ from the resulting stack. These two exterior outputs are the same on both sides. What lies between them is precisely the original rule $u\to v$, counted once even if a side is empty. Starting inside a code causes no exception. Every positive binary bubble therefore decodes to a positive original bubble, and encoding gives the converse. This use of the code reflects the **whole context predicate** on 2-computads, including histories not given by encoding an old expression. [Stack action and typed encoding](../answered/semistrict-surface-conservativity-2026-11-24.md#researcher-response-113)

Choose two internal outgoing edges from a branching vertex $x$. Follow each by a shortest return to $x$ to obtain distinct first-return paths $p,q$. Substitute them for $P,Q$ and place all rules at $x$. Any history from an empty path can move only if it starts at $x$. Inductively each visited path is a concatenation of $p,q$. Its visits to $x$ are exactly the boundaries between these paths, so even an empty-input step starts at a block boundary. Each matched nonempty rule consumes whole blocks. Cutting at the visits to $x$ recovers the binary history, preserving positivity. This proves hardness on the specified graph; enumerating finite histories gives the upper bound.

### When two accesses to a site remain distinct

Use the forgetful fibre and batch isotopy of [Responses 66](#researcher-response-66) and [67](#researcher-response-67). Fix a serial representative. Erase wires while keeping every gate point, signed seam and moving site disk. This includes the actual open one-probe spacetime in the flat one. First consider one adjacent cut and the disk of its site, split at a collared circle meeting its rim wires transversely. The flat cut is the union of the punctured disk and the punctured exterior along that circle. The circle injects in both fundamental groups because the disk contains a gate. In the actual cut use the faces of the two halves and glue along the accessible rim intervals, or along the whole rim at a point site.

Each half-face injects on fundamental groups in the corresponding flat half. Indeed each bounded complementary component of that planar face contains a gate point, or contains the excised disk on the exterior side. To see this, a finite component of the removed wire graph disjoint from both the boundary and the gates would have to be a closed gate-free wire, impossible by progression in drawing height. Boundary-attached graph joins the complement across that boundary. Pick one retained puncture per bounded hole (a point in the excised disk suffices for its hole). Filling everything except the chosen punctures maps the face's disjoint access meridians to a free basis. This proves injectivity, also for faces disjoint from the rim.

There is a stronger statement about paths. Suppose a path in a half-face with endpoints on the accessible rim becomes homotopic relative to its ends to a rim path in the flat half. It is already homotopic in the face to an accessible rim path. For a point site the whole rim is available and half-face injectivity proves this. For a wired site take an arm from each rim end to its first gate, or the entire chord for a through wire. In the exterior an arm can instead escape to the outer boundary. No exterior wire can run directly between two rim ends: after contracting the site such a wire would go forward in drawing height from the marker back to itself. The arms are proper arcs in the corresponding flat half, with distinct coordinates for different arcs even if they end at the same puncture. Intersection numbers with each oriented arc are invariant under a path homotopy fixing the two endpoints off the arms. The actual path has zero intersection. On pushing a rim traversal just inside the half, a single-ended arm contributes one signed unit; a through chord contributes opposite units at its two ends.

Read the rim ends in cyclic order, the bottom in spatial order and the top in reverse. A traversal winding at least one full turn in either direction meets every single-ended arm with the same sign on each visit. At least one such arm exists under the stated condition: a nonempty noncrossing perfect matching on the circle has a cyclically adjacent matched pair. A shorter, nonempty sequence of crossed ends could have total vector zero only if they were all matched in pairs within that consecutive sequence. The endpoints of an innermost pair would then be adjacent. A through chord joins bottom to top, so the only possible adjacent pairs are precisely the two extreme pairs in the criterion. In the exterior all arms are single-ended. It follows on either side that a zero-vector rim path reduces to a path in one accessible interval. Half-face injectivity now gives the required homotopy there. Conversely an adjacent matched pair gives a rim traversal crossing precisely its two ends with zero vector, including the full-turn case on two ends. This converse concerns the access test; the calculation below distinguishes actual outcomes when it fails.

### From local paths to the configuration fibre

Here is how to use this relative path statement when several tie faces continue into the *same* cut face. Split the cut into halves as above. The incidence graph has vertex spaces the half-faces and edges the rim intervals or circles. Edge groups inject in vertex groups, including at a point site by the nontrivial flat peripheral. In the universal cover the incidence graph is a tree, by the amalgam normal form. Map this tree to the flat cut tree. Two incident edges at a lifted half mapping to the same edge would give a half-face path between their rim positions flattening to a rim path. The relative path statement identifies the two lifted edges already. The tree map is therefore locally injective and embeds, and its vertex stabilizers inject by half-face injectivity. In particular if a cut path with endpoints in exterior half-faces can be homotoped into the *flat* exterior, its lifted endpoints are on one flat exterior vertex. Their actual exterior vertices coincide by tree injectivity. The path can consequently be homotoped into that actual exterior half-face.

Next split the spacetime at the event times. The vertex spaces are cut faces and each temporal edge space is an exterior half-face at the corresponding tie. Seams transport the chosen positions. All edge groups inject: in the flat cut this follows from the disk peripheral, and actual exterior groups inject even after flattening. The cut path statement just proved is the no-fold condition at a temporal vertex, separately for the preceding and following ties (their images are different temporal directions). Thus each actual temporal tree embeds in the flat temporal tree and cut stabilizers inject. The resulting map on one-probe fundamental groups is injective, and both spaces are aspherical since their trees of spaces have contractible lifted vertices and edges. This proof also covers components that meet neither end of the history.

The flat fundamental group is free. In serial order a tie is a plane punctured at the stationary gates and one site marker. On passing to the next cut, the marker maps to the peripheral product of its nonempty output packet; choose the same access stems for the stationary gates. This product belongs to a free basis together with the stationary generators and all but one of the packet generators. Thus gluing the next cut adds a free factor of rank one less than the packet size. Starting with the initial punctures gives rank equal to the initial gate count plus the sum of those increments. The original component groups are subgroups of this free group.

For clarity, group injectivity here suffices in place of a retraction of one-probe spaces. For a connected actual component and its flat target take their contractible universal covers. Distinct lifts of the fixed named punctures remain distinct by fundamental-group injectivity. Puncturing each cover at all lifts leaves it simply connected by general position. By excision its reduced homology is free in degree two on the individual meridian spheres and vanishes elsewhere. Joining the spheres to a basepoint gives a wedge equivalence by the homology form of Whitehead's theorem. Inclusion sends each sphere to its own meridian with the induced orientation. The pinch onto the corresponding wedge summands splits this map up to based homotopy. Thus punctured component inclusions inject on all positive groups, including the fundamental group from before puncturing. Use the forget-last-point fibration and its proper-ray section as in [Response 63](#researcher-response-63). Induction gives injectivity on all positive groups for ordered configurations in one component. If several components are occupied, forget the probes in all but one at a time. The degree-wise coordinate bound is that of the same response.

Given a surface witness, erase the probes. Once its unmarked difference fills raw, lift the original difference to the fibre by exactness. The occurrence lifts and coordinate specializations of [Response 69](#researcher-response-69) test this fibre element in the flat total spaces. The flat initial-collar section there ensures that vanishing in those totals implies vanishing in the corresponding flat fibres. The injections just proved then give raw vanishing. The six surfaces pass the flat tests by [Response 48](#researcher-response-48). With one name per occupied component the fibre itself has zero higher groups by asphericity, giving the stronger degree-six-and-above conclusion on an unmarked class with trivial higher groups.

Take parallel wires across the entire site, place nonempty lists of unary gates on them on both sides of a single event, and put a probe in an interior gap. Before and after the event its strip is simply connected. At the tie the site spans the strip, leaving two accessible ends in drawing height. The spacetime graph for this component has two vertices and two interval edges, hence fundamental group infinite cyclic. Its generator passes the input gates on the gap side and returns past the output gates. This component reaches an end, so the collar section of Response 69 detects its generator in the raw total too.

**Flattening detects that generator exactly when the union of the occupied gate lanes on both ports meets both sides of the gap.** To calculate it, push the probe through each positioned list, then return along the same exterior reference side of the whole packet. Identify the two packet peripherals in the flat amalgam and divide the two resulting words. In abelianization the comb for a port counts once, with a common sign, precisely the gates on one side of the gap. The sole relation identifies the sum of the input meridians with the sum of the output meridians. The difference vanishes only if both lists count nothing or both count everything. In the first case the two combs are already trivial; in the second they both traverse the whole packet peripheral with the same orientation. Hence vanishing in these cases holds for the actual words. For instance a two-wire site with its only gate on wire 1 on each port has an invisible raw generator in the middle gap (wires numbered from 0). Moving the output gate to wire 0 detects it, although neither port alone has gates on both sides. An invisible generator limits this flattening test; its surface filling is a separate question.

### Exact kernels across any number of strip changes

Fix an interior spatial gap in the full-width unary strip of Response 75. Take \(m\) full-width changes and nonempty lists of gates at its \(m+1\) cuts; repeated lanes and different reading orders are allowed. Use the specified common reading at each intervening cut. Mark each cut as left-only, right-only, or mixed. Give each mixed cut its *own* identifier, even when two cut lists are identical. Let \(d\) count the resulting distinct identifiers, including the left-only and right-only identifiers that actually occur. Then the raw one-probe rank is \(m\), the flat image rank is \(d-1\), and flattening is faithful exactly when neither single-side identifier occurs twice. In the consecutive loop basis \(u_1,\ldots,u_m\), normal generators of the kernel are the products \(u_{j+1}\cdots u_i\) from the first occurrence \(j\) of each repeated identifier to each subsequent occurrence \(i\).

Indeed, the actual space has a simply connected strip at each cut and two tie intervals per change. Use the lower tie edge to transport basepoints along the history. Crossing the input cut to the upper edge and coming back through the output cut gives the consecutive free basis. In the flat space choose the same exterior reference side of the packet throughout. The corresponding reference paths through a tie transport to the two adjacent cuts, so the image of \(u_i\) is \(c_{i-1}c_i^{-1}\), where \(c_i\) is the positioned gap comb followed by the inverse reference arc at cut \(i\). Van Kampen identifies the full packet peripheral \(z\) at all cuts. Thus the flat group is the free product of the cut groups amalgamated along their common primitive cyclic subgroup.

A single-side comb is either trivial or the same oriented full peripheral, with opposite side types giving the two different values. At a mixed cut, the abelianization of the comb counts a proper nonempty subset of the gates. It is independent of the total peripheral vector, so the comb and \(z\) do not commute (commuting elements of a free group are powers of a common element). They freely generate a rank-two subgroup. The amalgam normal form now says that all mixed combs and \(z\) together form a free basis of their subgroup: each two-generator subgroup meets the other cut groups along the amalgamated cyclic factor. In this basis the differences from one fixed comb to all the other distinct combs are freely independent. If a comb is trivial choose it as the reference; otherwise replace each other basis letter by its difference from the chosen one. The products \(u_1\cdots u_i\) are a basis of the raw ladder group and map to exactly these differences, with repetitions and the identity for recurrences of the initial comb. Identifying the repeated products and killing those identities proves the kernel formula.

For width two, cuts \([1],[0,1],[1]\) in the middle gap give consecutive images \(z^{-1}b,b^{-1}z\). Both survive and their product dies. This gives a **raw degree-five nonfilling** since the component reaches an end and its collar section injects the fibre. There is a higher example on the same movie with two probes. For any graph-type orientable one-probe component with group \(G\), forgetting the second probe has aspherical base and fibre the component punctured at the first probe. Its universal cover is contractible punctured at the \(G\)-orbit of the first probe. Thus \(\pi_2\) of the two-probe configuration is free abelian on the meridian spheres indexed by \(G\). With compatible lifts, flattening to another graph-type component maps the sphere indexed by \(g\) to that indexed by its image. In this example the difference of the spheres indexed by \(1\) and \(u_1u_2\) is a nonzero degree-six class that dies in the flat test. The end collar again detects it in the original raw total. Neither calculation alone decides an interchange-surface filler.

## Researcher Response 82

**One free probe in the Hopf-link exterior gives raw fillers at every parallel old boundary in degree six and above over the two-event history below.** This settles those queries for all ten ordinary surfaces. For arbitrary finite structural histories there is an exact decision of when a single probe adds any higher raw obstruction, even when its component has nontrivial fundamental group.

Let \(C\) be its one-probe component and \(G=\pi_1 C\). There is a computable integer \(r\ge0\) such that \(\pi_2 C\cong\mathbb Z[G]^r\) as a deck module. Its universal cover has the homotopy type of a wedge of 2-spheres indexed by \(G\times\{1,\ldots,r\}\). In particular \(r=0\) decides asphericity. For one probe, collapsing the structural history to the point events selected by [Response 80](#researcher-response-80) detects its contribution in *every* degree \(n\ge6\) exactly when \(G=1\) or \(r=0\). If neither holds, it loses a class in each such degree. With two or more probes Response 80's simple-connectivity condition is necessary already in degree six. These are tests for the specified detection map. A lost raw class need not have a filler on an interchange surface.

### Counting spheres in an embedded core

Take the compact connected PL core \(K\subset S^3\) of the chosen component, with nonempty boundary, as in [Response 77](#researcher-response-77). A PL sphere in its interior is reducing precisely when some original boundary component lies on each side. Indeed the sphere cuts \(S^3\) into two balls. A side with no boundary of \(K\) is wholly contained in \(K\); if both sides contain original boundary, neither ball fills the sphere in \(K\). An embedded core with connected boundary is therefore irreducible. An irreducible core of this kind is aspherical: the orientable sphere theorem gives \(\pi_2=0\), and the simply connected cover of its 2-spine then has zero reduced homology. [Hatcher, sphere and Schoenflies theorems](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

If all \(b\) boundary components are spheres, set \(r=b-1\) by the ball description in Response 80. Otherwise fill the spherical boundary components and count one extra sphere for each filling. On a piece with positive-genus boundaries only, test for a reducing sphere. If one is found, cut along it, cap its two copies, and recurse on the two resulting pieces, counting one extra sphere for this split. Each capped piece embeds in its own three-sphere, since its cap can replace the whole ball on the far side. Each has a nonempty proper subset of the original boundaries. Termination follows from this strict decrease. An irreducible piece contributes zero.

To verify the count, puncturing a compact connected 3-manifold with boundary adds a wedge summand \(S^2\), with the puncture sphere representing that summand. Join the puncture ball to a disk in an original boundary by a narrow regular neighborhood of an arc. This larger ball meets the rest along a disk. Filling it back before puncturing is a collar change; after puncturing it has the homotopy type of its puncture sphere. Gluing along the disk proves the relative wedge description. It follows in the same way that forming an interior connected sum of two pieces each with boundary gives their wedge and one 2-sphere: on each punctured side identify the indicated sphere summand with the sphere on the other side. This is a homotopy pushout along collars. Repeating the construction writes \(K\), up to based homotopy, as a wedge of the aspherical terminal pieces and the \(r\) extra spheres. The wedge of the aspherical pieces has contractible universal cover, by the tree of copies for a free product. Each extra sphere now lifts at every deck element. This gives the asserted deck module and the wedge description.

The reducing-sphere step is effective on a finite triangulation. If an orientable triangulated compact 3-manifold is reducible, there is a reducing **vertex normal sphere**. Enumerate the embedded vertex normal surfaces in standard coordinates. For each connected closed sphere, label each edge by its intersection number with that normal surface modulo two. Integrate along the 1-skeleton from one vertex to colour all vertices by side; integration is consistent since the sphere separates in \(S^3\). Read the colours on the real boundary components. Both colours must occur to certify a reducing sphere. This avoids a ball-recognition subproblem and also gives independently replayable positive certificates. [Jaco–Tollefson, Lemma 5.1](https://doi.org/10.1215/ijm/1255986385) · [Lackenby, Theorem 5.4 for compact manifolds](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/lackenby/pol23113.pdf)

With \(m\) named probes in \(C\), the fibre in the forget-last-point fibration is \(C\) minus \(m-1\) points. Its group is still \(G\) and its sphere count is \(r+m-1\). The proper-ray section splits the positive homotopy sequence. Thus as *abelian groups* for \(k\ge2\),
\[
 \pi_k\operatorname{Conf}_m(C)\ \cong \bigoplus_{i=0}^{m-1}
 \pi_k\!\left(\bigvee_{G\times\{1,\ldots,r+i\}}S^2\right).
\]
In degree two this gives \(mr+\binom m2\) additive copies of \(\mathbb Z[G]\). Use the product over occupied components and the section of [Response 79](#researcher-response-79) to include these groups in the actual raw total. In particular, with one probe per occupied component, all \(r=0\) reduces each of the ten surface tests in every degree from six on to the unmarked query. When \(G=1\) the pure comparison is an equivalence on the fixed configuration fibre as in Response 80. The remaining one-probe case has \(r>0\) and \(g\ne1\) in \(G\). For any sphere summand the translated sphere \(a_g\) and \(a_1\) are different wedge letters. Their difference, bracketed on the left \(k-2\) times with \(a_1\), is nonzero in \(\pi_k\) by the tensor coefficient calculation of [Response 77](#researcher-response-77). Both translate stems map to the same based class in the complement of point events, since that target is simply connected. This proves the one-probe necessity and explains why one probe can suffice to expose the limitation.

### Two histories with the same ordinary homology

Take a stationary 2-scalar, a birth of two 2-scalars beside it, then a death of those two. In the regular gap read the three strands as stationary, first daughter, second daughter. Its two ends join *at* infinity in the compactification, while the two daughters and their caps close to the other link component. Removing this link in \(S^3\) already removes infinity. An empty seam gives the two-component unlink. Closed support in global degree \(r\) cannot contain this element if \(r<g(P)\). This applies to coherence cases as well as operations and to heads at converted types. On a smaller tree evaluate the generic faces by recursively evaluating their constituent heads at the given tuple; every admitted constituent head again has small bound arity. A term on the actual ambient computad then uses the same formation rule with the same syntactic tuple; there is no head test on the ambient table. On a tape, every consecutive pair of updates shares the head, including its first and last use at the whole-tape ports. Hence it has just one temporal order. Different tapes can have any joint schedule respecting their orders. At a regular or active cut each live tape is one closed connected planar component with no holes or internal automorphisms; a tape at its outer site is just a point marker. Its lower diagram groupoid, for all the tapes together, is equivalent to the planar configuration groupoid of one point per tape. Select the head on an unchanged tape and the active marker on a changing tape. Each local update expands that marker to one head on each side, while the two whole-tape caps expand to no representative on the empty side. These selections commute with transport and disjoint expansions: restrict each packet braid to its specified representative. Equivalently put each fixed interval spelling in a small disk about its head, using the ordered ports for a changing interval. This gives equivalences on the schedule coefficients and their refinement maps. Consequently the raw component at empty ends is that of finite point lifetimes with unary beads. By [Response 91](#researcher-response-91) selecting their starts is a weak equivalence on named components to the configuration of one free point per tape. An unnamed loop that permutes tapes permutes starts, and within one tape its ordered events are fixed.

The map to pure points on this component is available to the surface itself: send all gates to point-only fits, the starting rule to one free 3-scalar with those fits, and all other rules to point-only comparisons. The preceding calculation shows that this very substitution detects raw differences. Conversely any accepting program embeds the pure test by the copying argument. Thus on a halting input, reflection at empty ends in the chosen degree is **equivalent** to reflection for the single pure 3-scalar in that degree. On a nonhalting input every such higher boundary fills raw. This proves the conditional hardness statement without assuming or constructing a binary-interchange filler for a collision class.

## Researcher Response 94

**For an ordinary finite point-rule 3-computad at the written ends \(e=1_{1_x},e\), it is P-complete to decide whether a raw degree-five obstruction with trivial occurrence transport exists.** This happens exactly when some returning program has an undirected cycle in its gate incidence graph. Parallel edges count. If the answer is negative, all ten individual surfaces reflect in degree five at these ends. If positive, the computad realizes the entire fixed mixed scalar test of Responses 44–45 at these *empty* ends, in every degree from five on. In particular its named raw fundamental groups contain \(F_m^k\) for every finite \(m,k\). The subgroup consists of motions of \(k\) probes around selected gate strands. Its existence alone leaves open whether a given surface fills one of those motions.

### Deciding which programs carry a cycle

Give each point colour a plain and a marked copy. For each rule take its plain version and one version for each pair of distinct incident port positions, marking just those two. The two positions may be on the same side. Compute all transitions occurring on zero-to-zero runs in the resulting net, and ask whether any version with marked ports occurs. A realizing run matches occurrences by the decorated colours, as permitted by the actual planar exchange paths of [Response 92](#researcher-response-92). On forgetting the decorations its marked edges have degree two at precisely the marked events, with no boundary endpoint. Any nonempty such finite graph contains a simple undirected cycle. Conversely, on an actual closed movie with a cycle mark precisely its edges, following their addresses through all signed seams. Reading this decorated movie gives the required run. This equivalence accounts for both the return of the entire program and the pairing of equal colours.

For explicit ordered port lists the decoration has polynomial size, and the set of zero-cycle transitions is polynomial-time computable. For the lower bound use nullability of a context-free grammar with only nonterminals on right-hand sides (the reduction in the cited paper). Binarize long right-hand sides with fresh symbols in logspace. For each production put one rule from its left-hand symbol to its right-hand list. Add fresh colours \(c,d\) and rules \(\emptyset\to S c,\ c\to dd,\ dd\to\emptyset\), where \(S\) is the start symbol. Add an independently available \(\emptyset\to\emptyset\) rule, so a positive return is promised in both cases. If \(S\) is nullable, expand one derivation tree and close the two daughters of the same split together, giving a bigon. Conversely any non-isolated event in a closed history requires a start birth, and the descendants of the \(S\) born there give a complete derivation of the empty word. Grammar rules have only one input, so the descendants of distinct starts cannot merge. This proves hardness even with at most two positions per side and only one binary-input rule. [Drewes and Leroux, Theorems 6.2–6.3](https://lmcs.episciences.org/1616/pdf)

If no cyclic return exists, every component of every returned incidence graph is a tree. Iterated leaf contraction of [Response 91](#researcher-response-91) leaves one isolated event per tree, including originally isolated events. At empty ends the named space is thus a configuration of points in three-space, simply connected. With repeated names a surface witness forces agreement of transports by occurrence lifting, which gives a raw filler in degree five. More generally, in this forest case, if any positive return exists then in each degree from five on empty-end reflection is equivalent to the pure free-3-scalar test. For the reduction to that test, lift the surface witness to occurrence names and retain one event per tree under the contraction, then fold colours (a null filler would lift). For the converse substitute a positive return for the free scalar as in Response 92. With no return all these boundaries fill.

### Putting a mixed test between two empty ends

Let \(P:e\to e\) be a returned movie, and choose an edge on a simple cycle in its trace \(G\). In an interior regular cut along that edge let \(h\) be its point colour. For a mixed test with \(m\) stationary points put \(m\) split copies of \(G\) side by side, and insert a long constant time interval at the chosen cut. Use a disk in the middle interval containing precisely the distinguished live gate of each copy. This placement is possible even with many other live gates. Place the marked points near distinct boundary arcs of the disk, in disjoint small neighborhoods straddling those arcs. Inside each neighborhood carry the cut configuration by a planar path to one point just inside the disk and all other cut points outside. Use the reverse path before the suffix. Each complete graph is contained in its own three-ball, and standard stems to the distinguished points can run through the common exterior before entering those balls.

Substitute \(h\) for the stationary 2-scalar and \(P\) for the free 3-scalar. In the middle first whisker by the other stationary gates outside the disk, then compose with the fixed prefixes and suffixes. Use planar boundary fits to the ordered cut ports. All these are raw operations available on a witness for each surface. If the fixed stationary path represents a braid, append its inverse to the mixed history first, with the prescribed endpoint fits. This is transport by a planar isomorphism up to raw higher cells. The resulting identity braid component of fixed-end planar paths is contractible, so one may compute its configurations at the stationary representative. In particular the use of a plain middle chamber does not restrict which mixed braid summand is tested. For \(m=0\) the pure substitution already suffices.

Here is the detection argument. Write \(U=(D^2-\{p_1,\ldots,p_m\})\times(0,1)\) for the chamber and \(Y=\mathbb R^3-\bigcup G_i\) for the one-probe complement of the fixed structural copies. Site disks and their collared expansions give the graph-complement model as in [Response 86](#researcher-response-86). The inclusion on fundamental groups is split injective. Splitting spheres give \(\pi_1Y=*_{i}\pi_1(\mathbb R^3-G_i)\) by van Kampen. In each factor linking with the chosen oriented cycle maps to \(\mathbb Z\) and sends the selected meridian to one, after orienting the cycle. The based meridians of the chamber enter their respective factors along the chosen stems. Taking the free product of these linking maps gives a left inverse to \(F_m\to\pi_1Y\). This is why the mixed puncture must surround the selected strand individually.

For a finite set \(Q\subset U\) the map \(U-Q\to Y-Q\) is injective on every positive homotopy group. Deleting points preserves the fundamental groups in dimension three. Upstairs the universal cover of \(U\) is contractible, and distinct lifts of \(Q\) enter distinct lifts on the target by the group injection. Both punctured covers are simply connected and have the homotopy type of wedges of 2-spheres by the spine argument of [Response 82](#researcher-response-82). In the target the little spheres at *all* lifts form a summand of integral second homology. Indeed the relative sequence and excision inject their free group into second homology since the unpunctured cover has zero third homology, and its cokernel is the free second homology of that cover. The source has exactly the little-sphere basis. Choose a target basis extending the included spheres and realize the resulting projection by a map between the wedges. Its composite with the lifted inclusion is homotopic to the identity, as can be checked on each source sphere. This proves detection in degrees above one as well.

For ordered configurations, forget the last point and induct on their number. These fibrations have sections on both open manifolds, for example by parking the new point sufficiently far out on a proper ray; hence fibre homotopy injects into total homotopy. If a class maps to zero, its projection is zero by induction, so it comes from the punctured fibre, where the preceding paragraph detects it. This proves the assertion for the *specified geometric inclusion* on configurations. In degree one it embeds \(F_m^k\), the fundamental group of the ordered chamber configuration since the diagonals have codimension three.

Finally, were an expanded raw boundary to fill, lift from its named gate segments and events. Retain the complete structural graphs. In each inserted probe copy flatten its lower colours and retain one named event as a point using the occurrence substitutions of [Responses 52](#researcher-response-52) and [92](#researcher-response-92). This works even when the probe and the structural graphs use the same generators. On the inserted family the retained point lies in its own substitution box and contracts to the original probe position. The target fixed-graph fibre injects into its raw total by the named section of [Response 79](#researcher-response-79). Thus a filler would null the chamber class. For repeated probes any nontrivial permutation of copies is detected already by the permutation of their nonempty event sets. Taking one probe round one selected edge proves the positive direction of the degree-five criterion. An actual mixed surface failure would transfer at the same degree and for the same surface; in degree five this would also make recognizing its empty-end failure P-hard even on the promised-return family above.

## Researcher Response 95

**Existence of a named raw degree-five obstruction at the written empty 2-ends is halting-hard for ordinary finite 3-computads with one object and one generating edge.** This remains true under the promise that a positive empty-to-empty program exists. On the accepting inputs one obtains an exact degree-wise surface comparison with a single point-rule presentation at empty ends. Its two rules are pair birth and pair death of one 2-scalar colour. In particular a failure on the fixed mixed test, or more generally on this pair-rule test, would make recognition of failure for that very surface and degree halting-hard on ordinary 3-computads.

### A release controlled by the accepting configuration

In the wired tape construction of [Response 92](#researcher-response-92), change the output of the rule on the whole cleaned tape to two occurrences of a single fresh point gate \(d\) on the empty spatial path. Give them a pair-death rule. Write \(K\) for the one-object scalar presentation with only \(d\), a birth from the empty 2-diagram to \(dd\), and this death back to empty. In the wired presentation only the release of a cleaned tape can produce \(d\). A tape update consumes the previous head and its consecutive neighbours on that same connected interval. It cannot consume a free \(d\) or take tape letters from another interval. Thus every started tape in a return must have run to cleanup. This holds also if outputs of *different* releases are braided and consumed in the same pair death. Conversely a halting input gives a specified raw term from the literal empty 2-end to the written pair \(dd\), and the death closes it.

If there is no halt there are no positive returns, so all ten surfaces reflect at these ends in each degree \(n\ge5\). One can separately adjoin a free 3-scalar to promise a positive return. Then on a nonhalting input only its occurrences are possible in a closed history. Their named configuration space in three-space is simply connected. This still gives degree-five reflection for every surface by occurrence transport.

### Why the fixed pair-rule test is exact on a halting input

At the given empty ends fix any named returned history. Its tapes have unique births and named releases. Between birth and release every update on a given tape shares its unique head with the next update. At a regular cut the live structural components are disjoint intervals with their fixed ordered gate words and free \(d\)-points. At an update the corresponding interval has a distinguished active site in place of the old head. Project each such interval to its head or active site. The lower groupoid comparison of [Response 92](#researcher-response-92) works with the other points present: they are additional singleton components, the inverse puts each interval spelling in its own small disk, and restriction of a cabled braid keeps one representative per component. On the two sides of a release the expansion is respectively one tape representative and two independent \(d\)-points. Deaths have two such inputs. These identifications commute with disjoint batches and refinement. The resulting scalar history therefore has one freely starting incoming branch per release, with a fixed sequence of unary beads on it, and exactly the original signed seams on the pair strands.

By the unary and free-branch contractions of [Response 91](#researcher-response-91), shortening each incoming branch to its own release gives a weak equivalence on named components to its pair-rule history. This contraction follows the actual tape trajectory, so it allows turns around other tapes or previously released points. The projection has a substitution on surface terms: send the generating edge and tape gates and updates to point-only fits, retain \(d\), send tape birth to its point-only fit, release to the pair birth, and death to the pair death. At release the flattened tape has an empty planar diagram. Compose the point-only comparison from its literal writing to the blank before the pair birth, and use the indicated port fits at the other faces. On histories this reads precisely the shortened branch. A permutation of distinct tapes permutes their retained releases, and fixing a release fixes the entire linear sequence of events on its tape. Ordered ports detect the transports of the surviving strands. Thus a surface failure in the wired source gives a surface failure in \(K\) even with repeated names. In the other direction substitute the chosen accepting prefix for each pair birth of \(K\). Under the projection this inserts a point-only collar at the birth of each pair, contractible relative to its written boundary. This detects each original raw difference and carries any surface witness. Consequently accepting inputs reflect in degree \(n\ge5\) if and only if \(K\) reflects at empty ends in that degree, separately for each individual surface.

If an independent free 3-scalar was adjoined, the same argument keeps it on both sides. The pair rules already have a positive return to use for this extra scalar. In each inserted copy retain one named event and flatten its internal gates, leaving the old pair histories intact, as in [Response 94](#researcher-response-94). This detects differences on the enlarged test in the original pair presentation. Conversely any proposed raw filler of an old boundary in the enlargement specializes back by assigning the new generator its identity. Thus the accepting comparison is the same under the positive-return promise.

### Which probes remain after erasing the tapes

One accepting release followed by a pair death has a bigon. Response 94 gives a named nonzero loop at the written empty ends, with or without the optional free generator. This proves the unconditional hardness. Furthermore, on the accepting family **every tame link group occurs as a subgroup of a named raw fundamental group**. Use several accepting prefixes for the bottom caps of a plat, any signed middle braid on their released \(d\)-strands and the corresponding pair deaths as top caps. Every tame link has such a plat. After tape contraction the probe spacetime is three-space minus this link. One freely placed probe injects its fundamental group into the named raw total by [Response 79](#researcher-response-79); a closed pair program serves in place of the free probe via the same occurrence selection. This includes words with zero abelianization, even for a connected trace. [Birman, *On the stable equivalence of plat representations of knots and links*](https://doi.org/10.4153/CJM-1976-030-1)

For the conditional complexity statement use the family without the optional scalar: rejection fills raw and acceptance has precisely the fixed pair test for the chosen degree and surface. The mixed test embeds there by Response 94. In degree five the same lower bound holds on the promised-return family, since the rejection case still reflects. The six surfaces covered by the scalar-rule result of [Response 48](#researcher-response-48) therefore reflect on the entire wired family at empty ends, even on the link-group examples. The four ordinary binary surfaces containing interchange remain the relevant tests.

## Researcher Response 97

**At empty 2-ends, a single fixed pair-birth and pair-death presentation decides uniform degree-wise surface reflection for all scalar-rule computads whose returning components have at most one independent cycle.** This reduction holds for each of the ten individual ordinary surfaces in each degree from five on. The class allows arbitrary arities and signed braids. It is decidable in polynomial time from the presentation whether all its returns satisfy this graph condition. In fact the greatest possible cycle rank of a single connected returning component is zero, one, or unbounded (using zero if there are no returns). Deciding whether it is unbounded is P-complete, even with a cyclic return promised.

### Reduction of a specified query to pair rules

Use the actual incidence multigraph of the returned movie, with an edge for every gate segment transported through its seams. The cycle rank of a connected component with \(E\) edges and \(V\) vertices is \(E-V+1\). A connected component of rank one consists of one simple cycle with trees attached. On a named history, prune leaves as in [Response 91](#researcher-response-91). A tree leaves one free point. On a component of rank one, the surviving vertices have exactly two incident edges, even when the original events had more ports. Smooth all vertices with one surviving input and one surviving output. The remaining vertices are precisely births and deaths of pairs, connected by the restricted signed seams. There is at least one maximum and one minimum on each closed cycle because event time strictly increases along a gate segment. Different components may be linked with each other or knotted. Pruning did not assume a split embedding.

At the level of raw differences these operations are weak equivalences of the named history components. The occurrence lifts, erasures and identity fits in Response 91 also transport a witness on the chosen surface. Fold the remaining lower colours to a single point gate, all pair births to one birth, and all deaths to one death at the corresponding port fits. On a named component this last operation just changes labels. A purported raw filler of the folded boundary would lift from the chosen occurrence names, so folding detects the difference. For trees keep a separate free 3-scalar at first. It can then be replaced by the pair-birth/pair-death return of the fixed presentation \(K\) of [Response 95](#researcher-response-95). After lifting any proposed raw filler, preserve the old pair graph and read one distinguished event from each inserted copy as a free point. This recovers the original difference, including permutations between free copies via their disjoint event sets. Thus **even without a promise on the presentation**, one boundary with only tree and rank-one components can be tested for surface failure by reduction to \(K\): a failure at that boundary implies a failure on \(K\) in the same degree. For uniform reflection over the stated class the converse follows because \(K\) itself belongs to the class. In particular, if a surface passes the fixed pair test then any remaining empty-ended scalar failure must have a connected component of rank at least two. The result is a comparison of surface questions; the four binary surfaces with interchange on \(K\) are still open.

### Detecting two cycles in one component

Give each point colour marked and plain copies as in [Response 94](#researcher-response-94). Now at each rule allow no marked ports, or any choice of **two, three or four** distinct marked port positions. Ask whether some version with three or four actually occurs on a zero-to-zero run. If so the marked graph has minimum degree at least two on its incident vertices, and the component containing that event has a strictly positive sum of \(\deg(v)-2\). Its rank is at least two. Conversely, in a component of rank at least two choose a spanning tree and two edges outside it. Retain this tree with just those two extra edges and repeatedly prune its leaves. The resulting connected subgraph has rank two and minimum degree two, with \(\sum_v(\deg(v)-2)=2\). Its degrees belong to \(\{2,3,4\}\), including at least one degree above two. Mark precisely those ports. This proves the criterion even for parallel edges, and distinguishes arbitrarily many disjoint circles from two independent cycles in one component. The bounded choice of four positions gives polynomial growth in the explicit port lists. Computing the transitions of a zero cycle is polynomial time by [Drewes and Leroux, Theorem 6.2](https://lmcs.episciences.org/1616/pdf).

For P-hardness use the nullable grammar of Response 94, its source \(\emptyset\to S c\), and an independent pair-birth/pair-death system on a separate colour. The latter promises a cyclic return and always has degree two at every incident event. On the fresh branch from \(c\) use \(c\to ud,\ u\to dd,\ dd\to v,\ vd\to\emptyset\). On a nullable input one complete grammar derivation together with this branch gives the desired connected rank two: route the two daughters of \(u\) into the first merge, and the other \(d\) into the last merge. On a nonnullable input no source can occur on an empty-ended run, by the independent descendants of its \(S\). Only the rank-one pair subsystem then remains. All rules use at most two ports per side.

### Amplification without further generators

Given a returned graph with a connected component of rank \(b\ge2\), choose a nonbridge edge in it and a regular cut in the life of that edge. Run \(m\) copies of the prefix side by side. At the cut braid just the \(m\) chosen live occurrences by a cyclic permutation with all other occurrences fixed in the permutation, then run the suffixes. This is a typed seam: the chosen gates have identical colour and planar paths can realize any such permutation. Cutting the chosen edge in each component leaves each copy connected. Cross-joining its source to the next copy's target connects the \(m\) components into one while preserving the total numbers of edges and vertices. The connected rank is exactly \(1+m(b-1)\). All other components are unaffected in their abstract incidence. Equivalently, the one-probe meridian homology from a *single* compact connected obstacle can now have arbitrarily high rank, by Alexander duality; this cannot be explained by counting disjoint obstacles.

It reconstructs the three-copy splice as a signed movie and checks the new ranks against the independent spine Betti numbers. ## Researcher Response 98

**One fixed finite ordinary 3-computad suffices for all scalar-rule surface tests, with any arities, colours, signed seams and fixed 2-ends.** It has one object, no generating edge, one point gate \(h:1_x\Rightarrow1_x\), and just three 3-generators, written at the empty 2-diagram \(e\) and the row \(hh=h*_1h\):
\[
                 B:e\longrightarrow h,\qquad D:h\longrightarrow e,
                 \qquad T:hh\longrightarrow hh.
\]
Call this presentation \(U\). For each individual ordinary surface and each degree \(n\ge5\), reflection over **all** finite point-rule presentations is equivalent to reflection over \(U\). The same equivalence holds when both 2-ends are required to be the literal \(e\). A failure transfers at the same degree, with the same surface. Through degree four reflection is already known. This gives a fixed target also for histories with arbitrarily large connected cycle rank, which the pair-rule reduction of [Response 97](#researcher-response-97) did not cover.

### Encoding an arbitrary rule

Fold the original point colours to \(h\). Use \(T\) followed by \(D\) on its second output to implement a merge \(hh\to h\). Use \(B\) on the right followed by \(T\) to implement a split \(h\to hh\). Insert the raw right unit fits where a literal binary writing has acquired a blank factor. To implement a rule with \(r\) inputs, merge the first two positions successively until exactly one remains. For the case \(r=0\) use \(B\) to supply that one. Now create another position on the right with \(B\), use a distinguished occurrence of \(T\), and consume its second output with \(D\). From the one remaining output, split successively to give the original \(s\) output positions in their prescribed order. If \(s=0\), consume it with \(D\). Even a rule with both ports empty has its distinguished \(T\).

These are programs in the three displayed generators. Choose a reading of each original written port, with an actual planar comparison from the folded source writing to the input row, and from the output row to the folded target writing. Compose with those fits; point-only 1-pole changes are available from the graph case. This gives a substitution on the *whole source presentation*, hence on any proposed surface witness. The program for a single update has length linear in its explicit port sizes. For a fixed representative history it lives in the original site disk and preserves the seam outside that disk. In particular it requires no new point on either fixed 2-end.

### Reading a raw difference back from the three rules

The intermediate gates have a second interpretation after naming their individual occurrences. Interpret each original surviving segment by its original point colour. Within an inserted program read a packed gate as the full ordered row of input segments it represents, using a left bracketing. Read the successive output packets by the corresponding prefixes of the output row. Read each temporary extra position as the blank \(e\). The two inputs to an auxiliary merge thus read as rows \(A,C\) and its first output reads as their concatenation. Its second output is blank. Map this occurrence of \(T\) to the planar rebracketing and right-unit expansion for those rows. For a split take the reverse fits. All uses of \(B,D\) in these instructions have blank image at the particle port and read as identities with their written fits. When an original side is empty its temporary carrier is blank too.

Interpret the distinguished \(T\) as the **original 3-update**, fitted at the chosen input and output rows and whiskered on the right by the blank. In fitting it, use the inverse of the actual port-reading paths used in the encoding. Thus any braid used to select an order at a written port returns along the same path. These assignments are well typed because they apply to individual ordered ports in the named occurrence presentation. Assigning every occurrence of the folded colour the same row would not recover the old rule.

On the encoded family this reading is homotopic to the original at its fixed ends. An auxiliary merge reads as a planar expansion to the padded row, an identity at its blank factor, and the contraction back. A split reads the same stationary collar. At the centre the expanded update is the original update between those collars. In the generic 2-disc the stationary collar and the identity have raw 4-comparisons in both directions; in the generic 3-disc the full central operation and its variable have such comparisons as well. More geometrically, keep the ordered packet points in a small neighborhood of their gate, expand and contract each stationary row there, and shrink the resulting time collars to the original port germs. Successive packings use the same row order, so these contractions move no strand around another. At the centre exactly one original event remains. The written port transports cancel with their inverses. Choices of smaller nested disks and time collars can be made over subdivided compact parameter families relative to their faces, as in the named substitution and contraction arguments of [Responses 79](#researcher-response-79) and [91](#researcher-response-91). This construction commutes with disjoint site refinements; a moving disk carries all of its packet positions through the original signed seam. It gives the required homotopy on families, including families in higher degrees.

If the image of an old difference filled raw, lift the filler starting at its named segments and sites by [Response 52](#researcher-response-52). Read these packet assignments on that lift. At a loop a nontrivial permutation of original sites permutes their distinguished occurrences of \(T\). Segment transports on surviving strands are read at the original cuts and ordered ports. Thus a null image also has compatible occurrence transport before reading the filler. The composite just described then gives a raw filler of the original difference at its written boundary. Therefore the forward substitution detects raw differences while carrying surface witnesses. The converse universal implication follows from \(U\) itself being a scalar-rule computad. In particular this one presentation suffices for the ordinary binary-interchange questions on the full scalar-rule class. The six surfaces of [Response 48](#researcher-response-48) already pass it. An affirmative result on \(U\) in a fixed degree would discharge the scalar-rule tests in that degree in the reductions to this class; reflection on arbitrary wired presentations still has its separate structural tests.

### Structural fits of ordered 2-histories

A 2-history is the chronological list of applications of generating 2-cells to substrings of edge words, at specified offsets, with its initial word. Empty lists and empty substrings are allowed. These are the degree-two values in the free Gray structure, equivalently through degree two in $E$. At these poles choose a raw writing $N(H)$ of each list: whisker each declared gate at its position, fit its graph ends to the chosen intermediate words, and compose the resulting factors in list order. Work in the ordered categories $C_X(p,q)$ at parallel written 1-poles. Their objects are raw 2-writings, their arrows are raw 3-terms modulo mutual raw 4-reachability, and the order is forward raw 4-reachability. At fixed poles the fits we will use give a specified isomorphism between any two writings of the same list. They compose transitively, and are preserved by raw substitution **as these isomorphisms**, with the corresponding changes of written poles. They have identity strict 3-value. Their naturality with one moving input follows on its temporal row, and the pentagon and triangle follow by identity comparisons on rows of 2-discs. ## Researcher Response 101

**A single finite ordinary 3-computad tests uniform conservativity on all finite ordinary 3-computads.** Fix any of the ten individual surfaces and any degree \(n\ge5\). It reflects in degree \(n\) on all finite 3-computads if and only if it reflects in that degree on the computad \(W\) below. This includes wired histories, bounded faces, empty ports and arbitrary raw 3-attaching diagrams. Through degree four reflection is already known. Thus the same \(W\) suffices in all degrees and for all ten surfaces. In particular Q3(b,c) **on 3-computads** asks just for reflection at the old degree-five and degree-six types over \(W\). More generally, for finite \(j\)-computads, \(j\ge3\), in degree \(n\ge j+2\), one may fix \(W\) as the entire 3-skeleton and allow arbitrary higher attachments. The assertion is a reduction; answering reflection on \(W\) still requires controlling its raw and surface fillers.

Use one object, one loop wire \(f\), and six planar gates. Width \(r\) denotes \(r\) copies of the wire.
\[
 b:0\to1,\quad d:1\to0,\quad t:2\to2,\quad
 m:2\to1,\quad s:1\to2,\quad h:1\to1 .
\]

Define \(M_0=b,\ M_1=I_1,\ M_{r+1}=(M_r\otimes I_1);m\) for \(r\ge1\). The vertical mirror \(S_r\) uses \(d,s\) in place of \(b,m\) and reverses temporal order. Put \(N_{r,k}=M_r;h;S_k\). The 3-declarations comprise **15 pairs of directed variables** and **one distinguished variable** \(z:h\to h\). For each pair of diagrams below include a variable in each direction.

| Planar diagrams joined by a pair of variables | Number of pairs |
|---|---:|
| \(a\) and \(N_{r,k}\) for \(a:r\to k\) among \(b,d,t,I_0,I_1\) | 5 |
| \(h\otimes h\) and \(m;h;s\), and separately \(h;h\) and \(h\) | 2 |
| \((I_1\otimes m);m\) and \((m\otimes I_1);m\), and the two unit pairs \((b\otimes I_1);m\), \((I_1\otimes b);m\) each with \(I_1\) | 3 |
| The vertical mirrors of these three associativity and unit pairs | 3 |
| \(d;b\) and \(I_1\), and separately \(s;m\) and \(I_1\) | 2 |

The pairs are generators and impose no inverse equations. ## Researcher Response 103

**For ordinary 3-computads one can localize the unresolved surface question to adjoining just two pairs of 3-generators to a fixed presentation on which every old boundary of degree at least five already fills raw.** In the notation of [Response 101](#researcher-response-101) the pairs are
\[
                  I_0\ \rightleftarrows\ b;d,
             \qquad I_2\ \rightleftarrows\ m;s .
\]
The first creates or consumes a floating interval in a blank sector. The second puts a merge followed by a split on two bare parallel wires, or returns those wires to their identities. The arrows in each direction are separate generators. On the completed fixed presentation, every surface failure in degree five or above must involve an occurrence of one of these four generators in the common history of the tested boundary. At the two written empty 2-ends a positive history necessarily uses **both directions of the first pair**, even if it also uses the second pair. Degree-wise uniform reflection on this one presentation is equivalent to reflection on all finite 3-computads, separately for each of the ten surfaces.

### The connected ports

Keep the six planar gates of Response 101. Take the following twelve pairs of 3-declarations, each with both directions, and the distinguished directed variable \(z:h\to h\).

| Two port diagrams | Number of pairs |
|---|---:|
| Each of \(b,d,t\) and its packed form \(N_{r,k}\) | 3 |
| \(h;h\) and \(h\) | 1 |
| \((h\otimes h);m\) and \(m;h\) | 1 |
| Input-tree associativity and its output-tree mirror | 2 |
| \((b\otimes I_1);m\) and \(h\), and \((I_1\otimes b);m\) and \(h\); also both mirrored fork pairs with target \(h\) | 4 |
| \(s;m\) and \(h\) | 1 |

Every individual port contains a gate, is connected, and contains all its incident boundary wires in that component. This includes \((h\otimes h);m\) since the final merge connects the two inputs. Response 73 therefore supplies raw fillers of every parallel boundary from degree five on over this base. It gives the same conclusion at a history in the enlarged presentation whenever that history uses only base events. Of the two additional pairs only their identity faces fail the test. At the empty ends the first rule use must have an entirely blank input on a path of width zero. Only the forward floating-interval rule has it. The last use gives the reverse requirement. [Connected-port theorem, including its supported-history version](#researcher-response-73)

### How the two pairs suffice

One must in particular implement creation of \(h\) on a **single** bare wire. Apply the zero-width interval creation beside that wire, then the two-wire rule between its birth and death. Up to ordinary planar rectangle and unit fits this gives the program
\[
 I_1\longrightarrow (b;d)\otimes I_1
 \longrightarrow (b\otimes I_1);m;s;(d\otimes I_1)
 \longrightarrow h;h\longrightarrow h.
\]
The penultimate step uses the left input-unit and left output-unit pairs on the two connected halves. Reversing the steps gives \(h\to I_1\). It follows that the required blank-scalar port comparison \(I_0\to b;h;d\) can be made by interval creation and this one-wire program between its gates, and conversely. Likewise any of the input/output unit pairs and the fork cancellation \(s;m\to I_1\) in the port algorithm of Response 101 can go via \(h\).

For horizontal combination, follow \(h\otimes h\) by the two-wire creation and apply the connected absorption pair to the resulting merge. This gives exactly \(m;h;s\). The last missing comparison is \(d;b\to I_1\). By ordinary interchange \(d;b\) can be read as \(d\otimes b\), with intermediate width zero. Apply the horizontal packing algorithm to these two leaves and then convert the resulting \(h\) to \(I_1\). This construction only packs two horizontally adjacent leaves; it uses no instance of the vertical cancellation it implements. Reversing the independently declared steps supplies the opposite comparison. All other port instructions are among the connected pairs or their rebracketings. This proves coverage of the old compiler.

For raw detection, use these programs *inside the labelled encoding* of Response 101. When creating \(h\) on a bare packet, the temporary interval carries the old empty word at its object. The two-wire connector initially compares two identity wires with packing and splitting the same two packet words. Decode these tree gates by graph fits; the two intermediate \(h\)'s in the one-wire construction both read as identities on the original packet up to those fits. When absorbing two genuine diagrams at a horizontal node, the new central \(h\) reads their complete juxtaposition. The merge at the absorbing step is an invertible graph comparison on the ordered output wires. When cancelling \(d;b\), the two structural leaves involved read as graph fits on the empty word, so their packed composite has the required identity reading. In particular all auxiliary steps have invertible decoded images with the stipulated faces. The original input 3-generator is still represented by the unique distinguished update at the centre of its compiled program. The decoder, relative homotopy and final generator fold of Response 101 therefore apply unchanged in their stated dimensions. This also gives the corresponding fixed 3-skeleton reduction with higher declarations in degree \(n\ge j+2\) for finite \(j\)-computads.

**Reproduce.** Run `python3 tools/semistrict_surface_box_exceptions.py --agda-dir DIR` and `agda --safe --no-libraries -i src -i DIR DIR/TwoExceptionalPorts.agda`. The solver computes connected components from the positioned gates, gluing the actual input/output wire segments. It checks both ports of all 29 directed declarations by their two-way templates and centre. It expands all 30 directions used by the port compiler and replays them at their precise diagrams in the new library. It also compiles 30 full updates at different offsets. Agda checks the complete program \(I_1\to h\) at its literal type, including the rectangle moving the floating interval onto the two-wire cut, the graph-pole fits, and the rebracketing that exposes both connected contractions. Use `--presentation` for port diagrams and their component counts, or pass a source/target JSON query with `--certificate` for its expanded local moves. ## Researcher Response 104

**In the fixed universal presentation of Response 103, a failure in degree six or higher requires an exceptional event incomparable with another event by gate dependence.** At the written empty 2-ends the same necessity holds already in degree five, for all ten individual surfaces. At arbitrary ends, if each exceptional event is comparable with every other use, all degree-five boundaries fill raw except possibly when the first and last events create and consume a floating interval in faces with holes. In that residual case degree five reflects for the six surfaces of Response 48, and for each remaining binary surface it reduces to the single-free-probe mixed test of Response 44. In particular an exceptional event can sit next to an arbitrarily concurrent middle without producing a degree-six obstruction.

### Cutting at forced gaps

The following raw decomposition applies to **any** ordinary 3-computad. Name the events in a history and trace their gate segments through the actual signed seams. Order the events by transitive dependence through those segments. Form a graph by joining *incomparable* events, and take its connected components. These blocks are totally ordered: an event comparable to both ends of an incomparability edge lies on the same side of both unless it belongs to that block. Propagate along paths. Thus the poset is the ordinal sum of the subposets on the blocks. No simultaneous tier crosses between blocks.

Choose a regular cut between each consecutive pair. The choice within each open time gap is contractible, including for families by subdivision of the parametrized movies. The history component with its outer 2-ends fixed is obtained by matching the block histories over the planar groupoids at these cuts. More explicitly the evaluation to the product of intermediate diagram spaces has homotopy fibre, at the chosen diagrams, the product of the block spaces with both ends fixed. This follows also directly from the change-index construction: every batch and every permitted refinement belongs to one block; split the intermediate seam path at the chosen cut and concatenate the resulting independent strings. Splitting and concatenation are inverse up to the contractible cut choices, with the seam paths retained. Restrict to the components at the given based history. Every diagram space at a seam is a 1-type. Consequently in each homotopy degree \(k\ge2\) the actual fixed-end group is the **product of the corresponding fixed-end block groups**. In degree one the product of the block fundamental groups still injects; the remaining motion can run through the seam groups. Naming does not change higher groups; in degree one retain the occurrence transport. [Fixed-end coefficients and planar groupoids](#researcher-response-52)

A single-site block is a homotopy pullback of planar 1-types and is itself a 1-type. A block of events with positive ports satisfying the connected-port condition has homotopy-discrete fixed-end space by [Response 73](#researcher-response-73). Thus no degree-six or higher obstruction survives when every block is either a singleton or of this latter kind. In the universal presentation this proves the first assertion.

### The two possible outer events

More generally allow any number of Response 73 events, and additional events each having one blank gate list and a nonempty opposite list. Suppose each additional event is comparable to every other use. A blank-input event has no predecessor and must be first; a blank-output event has no successor and must be last. There is at most one of each. The positive middle, with all its possible schedules and signed seams, has homotopy-discrete fixed-end fibres. The outer site groups project injectively toward their nonempty sides: on gate braids the map cables the site strand by a nonempty packet, and retaining one member recovers it. Positioned gate braids detect planar loops.

There is also propagation through the entire positive middle. In its named incidence graph take all full directed paths from an incoming gate to an outgoing gate, including stationary paths. Replace each gate by the nonempty packet of paths passing through it. Each positive use becomes a planar change between two arrangements of the same path names. On cut groupoids the resulting cabling is injective on fundamental groups by restricting to one strand per gate. Hence the two endpoint braids of a loop through the middle, after their respective cablings, agree up to transport along the specified path program. If one vanishes the other vanishes. With both trivial the middle loop is trivial by its fixed-end result and the homotopy exact sequence. This uses the actual wire geometry before flattening for the fixed-end result. [Full paths through a concurrent positive middle](#researcher-response-70)

It follows that a loop of the whole fixed-end history is detected by its first site group when there is a birth, and dually by its last site group when there is a death. Indeed vanishing at one end propagates across the middle and then to the other site by nonempty-side injectivity. With zero seam braids there are no remaining block loops: the middle has discrete fixed-end fibres, and the singleton blocks with a nonempty side have discrete fixed-end fibres by that same injectivity. If an outer site is absent the corresponding end braid is already zero. There is no unseen permutation in this argument. The fixed initial positions and ordered outputs of the unique first birth, when present, determine middle events by tracing the unique consumer of a gate and the ordered outputs at that event. Every middle use has an input; the terminal death, if present, is distinguished by its order. This determines the names around a fixed-end loop.

If the blank side is on a **nonempty spatial path**, its site group injects even on that side. Here the site on the identity port has an incident strand, with the next neighbouring gate or the fixed rim at its other end. In a loop of the marked chart move its point representative along this very wire toward that end while retaining the other gate representatives. No other point lies on the open wire segment. At a neighbouring gate the representative can be taken in a short incident collar, which can be straightened to the prescribed side by progressiveness and the linear port order. Its braid is therefore the braid obtained by adjoining a close parallel copy of that gate, up to the fixed change of basepoint. At a fixed rim use a fixed nearby representative in its boundary collar instead. The collar lengths can be chosen small over the compact loop. Triviality after forgetting the site thus makes the full positioned gate braid trivial, which detects the marked chart loop. In particular a universally comparable two-wire exception contributes no residual degree-five case. For a blank side on the empty path, the kernel instead injects into, and is given by, the fundamental group of the face of the site: forgetting one point has that punctured face as fibre, and the base is a 1-type. ### One configuration for each lifetime of a face

Here is a more general statement for ordinary 3-computads. Fix a named component of histories from the empty drawing to itself. A closed positive port can replace a whole connected component. The ordered rim and connectivity ensure that each wired replacement preserves all incidences with the exterior. This is about spatial connectivity; the events updating one such component need not form a chain of gate dependencies.

There is one root face. Each bounded face in a connected drawing has a lifetime, from its first appearance in a written output until it disappears in a written input. Indeed each local exterior sector of a connected spanning port corresponds to the same sector of the marker star. Any identifications of these sectors by the rest of the drawing agree on both sides. The other faces are internal to the port. At a point site the marker has just one exterior sector. Thus the tie-to-cut maps on ambient face *sets* are injections, and a missed face is internal to that side. The same description holds at several disjoint sites; a newly created face is labelled by its event and its particular internal port face. A component born in a bounded face stays in that face of its parent throughout its life.
