### The bottom square for a projective label

Set \(L=m+1\), \(P=\mathbb RP^\infty=BC_2\), and \(Y_P=\Sigma^{m-1}P\). For its bottom class \(x\), we claim
\[
                   [x,x]=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\text{ is a power of two}.
\]
We will also need the following proof for the Moore space \(Y_M=S^m\cup_2 e^{m+1}\). For either \(Z=Y_P,Y_M\), vanishing of its bottom square is equivalent to the existence of a map \(f:S^{2m+1}\to\Sigma Z\) for which the degree-\(L\) mod-two class \(c\) on the mapping cone has nonzero square. The class \(c\) is the unique extension of the suspended bottom cohomology generator.

In fact \([x,x]=0\) extends the two copies of \(x\) on the wedge to \(\mu:S^m\times S^m\to Z\), since the product attaches its top cell by the Whitehead product of the inclusions. Take the Hopf construction on \(\mu\). Its top characteristic disk is \(D^L\times D^L\), with the two boundary pieces mapping into opposite cones on \(Z\). Lift \(c\) relative to each contractible cone. On the disk relative to the corresponding boundary piece, its pullback is the generator from the corresponding disk factor. Indeed restrict to that factor with the other coordinate fixed at a based point of its boundary. The resulting quotient map is the suspension of the restriction of \(\mu\) to that axis, and the bottom cohomology generator evaluates to one on \(x\). The two relative classes therefore multiply to the generator relative to the whole boundary. Its image is \(c^2\). The top relative class injects into absolute cohomology since \(f\) sends the integral fundamental class to zero, hence also its mod-two reduction. For \(Y_P\) this uses \(H_{2m+1}(\Sigma Y_P;\mathbb Z)=H_{m+1}(P;\mathbb Z)=0\), as \(m+1\) is positive and even. For \(Y_M\) the same vanishing follows by dimension. This gives the relative cup-product argument also when the target has cells above the bottom. [May, *A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology*, Chapter 24 §6](https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/CONCISE/ConciseRevised.pdf#page=225)

Conversely the pair \((JZ,Z)\) for the James construction gives the exact sequence
\[
 \pi_{2m} Z\longrightarrow \pi_{2m+1}\Sigma Z\longrightarrow
 H_m Z\otimes H_m Z\xrightarrow{\partial}\pi_{2m-1}Z.
\]
The first map is suspension, the tensor group is cyclic of order two, and \(\partial(x\otimes x)=[x,x]\), by the length-two quotient and relative Hurewicz in Response 163. If the square were nonzero, every \(f\) would be a suspension. Its cone would then be a suspension with zero cup products. Finally, stable maps in this degree have actual representatives because \(\Sigma Z\) is \(m\)-connected and Freudenthal gives surjectivity in degree \(2m+1\). Steenrod squares commute with cohomology suspension, so a stable nonzero \(Sq^L\) on the bottom gives \(Sq^L c=c^2\ne0\) on an actual cone.

If \(L=2^j\), the projective-space stable map \(S^L\to P\) of Cohen–Lin–Mahowald has nonzero \(Sq^L\) on the degree-one class of its cone. Suspending stably by \(m\) and applying the preceding criterion gives \([x,x]=0\) in \(Y_P\). [Cohen–Lin–Mahowald, §3, equation (3.1)](https://msp.org/pjm/1988/134-1/pjm-v134-n1-p02-s.pdf#page=21)

For the other direction suppose \(L\) is not a power of two. On the cone just constructed from a putative vanishing square, write \(t\in H^1(P;\mathbb F_2)\) for the generator, so \(c\) restricts to \(\Sigma^m t\). Restriction is injective below the new cell of degree \(2L\). Put \(r=2^{v_2(L)}\) and \(s=L-r\). Then \(s\ge2r\) and \(2r\mid s\). The Adem relation for \(Sq^r Sq^s\) contains \(Sq^L\) with coefficient \(\binom{s-1}{r}\equiv1\pmod2\), since the binary digit of \(s-1\) at \(r\) is one. Every other summand is a multiple of \(Sq^{L-j}Sq^j\) with \(1\le j\le r/2\). On \(c\) the left side and every right-hand term with \(j\ge2\) vanish, by restriction, stability and instability on \(t\). For \(j=1\), use \(Sq^{L-1}=Sq^1Sq^{L-2}\). The inner class \(Sq^{L-2}Sq^1c\) restricts to \(\Sigma^m Sq^{L-2}(t^2)=0\) since \(L\ge6\). Thus \(Sq^L c=0\), contrary to the Hopf construction. This proves the claim.

### Consequences for old judgments

Take \(m=n+1\) with \(L\) not a power of two. Then \(A=H_1K\). Each nonzero \(v\in A/2A\) admits a character \(A\to C_2\) carrying it to one. Realize the character by \(K\to P\) and suspend. Naturality sends \(q_Y(v)\) to the nonzero projective square just proved. Hence \(q_Y\) is an isomorphism for every such label. In particular, to test the entire family, take Response 163's finite reversible presentation of the local \(i\)-type \(BC_2\), one stationary colour, and the old comparison from the shell of the bottom square to zero. A failure anywhere gives a nonzero surface-null \(q_Y(v)\) at one puncture. The chosen character gives a raw substitution into the tester by the prescribed-face realization of maps of local \(i\)-types in Responses 158 and 163. The suspended Postnikov comparison is \((i+n+1)\)-connected, so the substitution retains the calculated degree-\((i+1)\) class. It takes the proposed filler to the tester. Conversely a filler there is itself a failure, because the square is nonzero. The first such case is \(n=4\), in output degree 13.

At dyadic \(L\), every bottom class carried by a map \(Y_P\to Y\) from its bottom generator has square zero. For instance, if \(d=m-n\) and the local \(i\)-type is \(K(C_2^b,d)\), each basis direction is carried in this way after passage to the local Postnikov section. Represent the suspended degree-one character by a map \(\Sigma^{d-1}P\to K(C_2,d)\), include a coordinate, and suspend by \(n\). Connectivity of the comparison with the Postnikov section again gives an isomorphism on the shell. Thus published insertion reflects at every old boundary in this degree for these presentations. Response 163 constructs finite testers of the required cyclic type.

### When order two alone forces reflection

For \(Z=Y_M\) and \(L=2^j\), \(j\ge4\), the criterion above says that its bottom square vanishes precisely when there is a stable map in stem \(2^j-1\) into the Moore spectrum \(M(2)\) whose cone has nonzero \(Sq^{2^j}\) from the bottom. This is the Adams filtration-one detection \(h_j e_0\). To see the identification, the sphere source has zero Hurewicz image for degree reasons and the nonzero primary extension detects filtration one. The bottom-cell inclusion carries the sphere's \(h_j\) to the extension with that bottom reading. There is no additional filtration-one class from the upper cell, since its sphere stem \(2^j-2\) is positive and even, and degree-one Ext of the sphere is generated by the \(h_k\) in stems \(2^k-1\). Miller's equivalence now says precisely that some element of order two in stem \(2^j-2\) is detected by \(h_{j-1}^2\). [Miller, *Kervaire invariant and Hopf invariant for the Moore space*](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/papers/hopf-kervaire.pdf)

Such elements exist in stems 14, 30 and 62. For the corresponding \(m=15,31,63\), every \(y\in A\) with \(2y=0\) extends from the bottom sphere to a map \(Y_M\to Y\), using a nullhomotopy of \(2y\). This allows any higher attachments consistent with the stated hypotheses. For \(m=127\) the same proof requires an **order-two** Kervaire class in stem 126. The existence theorem for a Kervaire class in that stem alone does not supply its order. For every dyadic \(L\ge256\), Hill–Hopkins–Ravenel exclude the requisite Kervaire class. The bottom square in \(Y_M\) is therefore nonzero, whereas the bottom square in \(Y_P\) vanishes. These give finite presentations with the **same** bottom group \(A=C_2\) and different \(T_{n,i}\), even with \(n=m-1\) fixed at each such dimension. Use the circle with a degree-two relation, completed through \(i\) by the inverse and round-trip attachments of Response 158, for the Moore case. Its extra \((i+1)\)-spheres do not affect the suspended shell. Use the finite cyclic \(i\)-type tester for the projective case. This proves that bottom homology alone cannot classify the raw obstruction in those dimensions. The Moore presentation would be an insertion counterexample if its nonzero shell admitted a published filler. [Hill–Hopkins–Ravenel, Main Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/0908.3724)

## Researcher Response 166

**For every scalar rank \(n\ge2\), every positive ordinary scalar-rule test for Q1(b) reduces, at the same degree and on the same surface, to one scalar \(a\) and one rule \(T:aa\to aa\).** Here a positive rule consumes and produces at least one scalar occurrence, with arbitrary multiplicities on the two sides. The history can have arbitrary dependence. For each fixed degree, reflection throughout this class is equivalent to reflection on this one computad. In particular Q3(b) in degree six on positive rank-three scalar computads requires only this tester. The number of uses of \(T\) is unbounded. This complements the two-use reduction for independent events in [Response 164](#researcher-response-164). For the one-sided class in which every rule has an output, add just \(B:e\to a\); for the dual class add just \(D:a\to e\). For unrestricted ports use all three. The unrestricted rank-two implication is [Response 98](#researcher-response-98).

### A conserved width adapted to the supported history

Fix a surface witness at old faces. Give its rule uses distinct names and then give its wires distinct names, propagating the input states and assigning each output its ordered port address. The two lifts preserve the witness and the heads and written boundaries of its raw faces. Both lifts matter when different uses of the same rule need different packet sizes. Write \(N\) for the resulting finite directed acyclic network. Use an ordered product for each port, recording the raw paths from its actual writing and using their inverses upon decoding. [Occurrence and state lifts, including empty ports](../answered/semistrict-surface-conservativity-2026-11-24.md#naming-events-before-wires)

For each wire choose a complete directed route through it. Extend at either end as long as there is an incident wire on the other side of that site. Double these routes if necessary so at least two routes pass every positive site. Set the width of a wire to the number of routes on it. Every wire now has positive width; at each positive site total input width equals total output width \(M\ge2\). Each side of a proper birth or death that has wires has positive total width. This already suffices for the reduction.

There is an exact width certificate for positive histories. Give each wire one obligation and each site two incomparable obligations. On a path, the incoming wire precedes either site obligation, and either site obligation precedes each outgoing wire. Take the transitive closure. A collection of complete routes covering these obligations can use each route at most once at a given site. Conversely a chain of obligations extends to a complete route, choosing connecting subpaths and extending to both ends. Thus the minimum conserved width under the stated wire and site requirements is the maximum size of an antichain of obligations. Explicitly, match left to right copies of strictly comparable obligations. A matching gives one fewer chain per match on joining successors; a chain partition supplies those matches in reverse. For a maximum matching, start an alternating search at the unmatched left copies. The obligations with reached left and unreached right copy are incomparable: all right neighbors of a reached left are reached, and comparabilities are transitive. In detail, if two selected obligations were ordered, the right copy of the larger would be reached. Every reached right has its matched left reached, and also its *own* left reached: if that left is matched forward, transitivity from the predecessor in the search reaches its matched right, otherwise it is a search root. Consequently the antichain size is the number of unmatched left copies. The solver gives the antichain and routes of this same size. In a positive network every complete route starts and finishes on an exterior wire, so this is the actual physical row width at every regular cut. For proper caps one site obligation suffices, and a site with neither port is treated separately. There the route count need not equal width at each cut.

### Substitutions at the written faces

Send an old named wire to its ordered packet of fresh scalar strands of the indicated width. In the reverse interpretation the first strand reads as that old wire and the others read as the scalar unit \(e\). Within a positive site the concatenated input and output packets have equal length. In its own disk use successive \(T\)'s on neighboring pairs, sweeping from right to left. Read the two outputs of each as the concatenated ordered old contents and a blank. The first physical strand now carries the whole old input. Use one distinguished \(T\) at positions one and two to perform the old update, with its whole output on the first strand. Sweep from left to right, leaving the required old output label or blank at each position and passing the remaining ordered suffix to the next strand. At width two the distinguished update can take the two given input packets directly to the two desired output packets. This uses one instruction at width two and at most \(2M-1\) in general. Each instruction has its own occurrence name and both its outgoing strands receive fresh names.

At a proper birth create the required physical strands using \(B\), one occurrence per strand. Read the first birth as the original event with its entire ordered output; the rest create blanks. Scatter as above. At a proper death gather its input then consume the strands with \(D\), reading the death of the carrier as the old event. At a site with both ports empty create and consume a single blank, reading the birth as the original free event. No such site occurs in either one-sided class. On a bypass strand use its packet throughout. These rules define a substitution on the supported named computad. In particular separate sites, including two simultaneous births, have disjoint programs. They impose no chronological choice between those sites on the surface witness.

For the reverse map, send every physical named strand to its assigned scalar word and every named physical rule to its indicated old update or ordered port fit. At an auxiliary sweep step the concatenated old lists on both sides agree, including their order. Their raw bracket and unit fits are obtained on the linear arity and can be made by collinear interval placements. At the unique distinguished step use the old rule with these fits at its actual poles. On the composite, each old wire is thus the old wire with units, each old event is that event in ordered collars, and each chosen external port-reading path returns by its inverse. The stationary collars contract relative to their ends: for a fixed list the inequalities on ordered disjoint little intervals are convex, and an empty list has a unique reading. Shrink the time collars of the one real update to its original germ. These contractions commute on disjoint disks and move with the disks along seams. Equivalently they agree on the faces of the free arrow attachments, giving a homotopy of the composite on named fixed-end families, transported at the written endpoints. This is the ordered-packet argument of [Response 98](#researcher-response-98) with the rank-independent linear fits of [round-one Response 108](../answered/semistrict-surface-conservativity-2026-11-24.md#forgetting-a-port-while-retaining-its-event).

Finally fold the physical scalar names to \(a\) and instruction names to their rule of the indicated arity. A surface witness folds forward. At degree \(k\ge n+3\) a raw filling in the folded tester lifts back from the common supported \((n+1)\)-history: incidence and port positions transport the very names used by the encoded faces. In the loop case nullhomotopy gives trivial name transport; in higher degrees use the same covering at the based globe. The reverse substitution and the preceding relative contraction then fill the original raw difference. Thus any failure transfers. Pure histories need only the scalar-name fold, by the same occurrence lift. For \(k\le n+2\) reflection is already known, by ordinary reflection through four at \(n=2\) and the arbitrary-port bound through \(2n-1\) at \(n\ge3\). Each tester belongs to the class it tests, giving the converse. The theorem leaves the surface judgment on the one-rule tester open.

### Retaining one stage detects the whole group

Lift the four strands and each use to occurrence names. Give the initial strands four distinct lane addresses. At every site transport these addresses from the two input positions to the two output positions in order, tracing any external permutations along the seams. Each site is now a pair from a four-element set. Two pairs are disjoint exactly when they are complementary. Read the events serially and divide the reading into maximal runs belonging to one fixed partition into two pairs. Within a run, the sites on either pair form one chain, independent of the other. Any pair in one run meets every pair in the next run. A common lane supplies a dependence path even when intermediate events intervene. Hence the dependence order is the ordinal sum of these runs. Swapping adjacent independent uses preserves this decomposition. A stage may use only one of its two pairs.

Let \(P=\bigwedge^2\mathbb Z^4\), on the oriented lane pairs. Write \(G_i\) for the fixed-end group of run \(i\). The two extreme cut maps \(L_i,R_i:P\to G_i\) have central image. All cuts of distinct runs are comparable. By the [cut presentation and seam calculation](../answered/semistrict-surface-conservativity-2026-11-24.md#researcher-response-90), the whole group is the product of the \(G_i\) with the central identifications \(R_i(p)=L_{i+1}(p)\). Contracting all named uses of one run straight through is a map \(f_i:G_i\to P\), with \(f_iL_i=f_iR_i=1_P\) (identity maps). Indeed each labelled wire goes to its lane; each rule goes to the identity on the two lanes with its ordered port fits. Every cut sphere reads as the oriented sphere of those same lanes. At rank three ordered configuration spaces are simply connected, so the endpoint transports chosen to fit the wires do not change this reading.

Retain run \(i\), contracting every other run straight through. This is a substitution after the occurrence lift: keep separate wire names through the successive cuts of the retained run, extending its initial names backwards and final names forwards along the lanes. A tuple \((g_1,\ldots,g_k)\) projects to
\[
       L_i(S_{i-1})\,g_i\,R_i(S_k-S_i),
       \qquad S_j=\sum_{h\le j} f_h(g_h),\quad S_0=0.
\]
If all projections are identities, applying \(f_i\) gives \(S_k=0\). Hence \(g_i=L_i(-S_{i-1})R_i(S_i)\). Their product telescopes to the identity by the seam identifications. This proves joint detection without a restriction on the length or the commutator depth of the original difference. Conversely each grid is itself a four-lane history. Thus degree-six reflection throughout this sector is equivalent, separately for each binary surface, to reflection on the grids. It also covers positive histories that the certified compiler of [Response 166](#researcher-response-166) puts on at most four lanes: smaller widths can be padded by stationary lanes with a retraction to the original ends.

For chains of lengths \(r,s\), index cuts by \((i,j)\in[0,r]\times[0,s]\). In each column use the sum \(u\) of its two tips, which continues across every site, and the first tip \(v_i\), specific to the current cut of that column. These are an integral basis; the second tip is \(u-v_i\). The within-column pair at each stage is central, as are the cross products involving at least one sum. The other basis letters \(x_{ij}=v_i\wedge v_j\), with the first factor in the left column, generate the graph group with commutations precisely for comparable grid positions. This follows by expanding both cut groups and single-site marker transfers in the displayed bases. The two extreme grid letters commute with the entire group as well. Each signed generator is realized by an actual pair sphere at its cut. The solver keeps the central coordinates and solves the graph word problem by cancelling powers separated only by commuting letters. This gives the exact raw test together with the run projections above.

In the abelianization, a nonzero coefficient can be isolated under straight-through contractions. For each of its specified local cut indices keep the event immediately before and immediately after that index, whenever present. After contracting every other event in the column, only that index projects to the selected new index. A persistent sum remains a sum and is distinct from the new local generators. Within-column pairs map to the corresponding within-column pairs. Thus the coefficient survives, even if the full word also had a commutator part. For a stage with one active pair all grid positions are comparable, so this already detects every failure there. At width at most three the binary event order is total. After padding to four, each run has only one active pair, since two disjoint active pairs would require four active lanes. No two distinct antidiagonal positions are comparable. For the \((i+1)\)-st left event use the cut word \(U_i=x_{i,d-i}x_{i+1,d-i}^{-1}\), for \(0\le i<d\). For the \((j+1)\)-st right event use \(V_j=x_{d-j,j}x_{d-j,j+1}^{-1}\), for \(0\le j<d\). Contracting the indicated use identifies the two positions and their first tips, so the corresponding word vanishes. Under the antidiagonal retraction these words read \(a_i\) and \(a_{d-j}\), respectively.

Begin with \([U_0,V_0]\), then bracket successively with the remaining \(U_i\)'s and \(V_j\)'s in increasing index within each list. The first two projected generators \(a_0,a_d\) are distinct. Each subsequent projected bracket is again nontrivial: the running element has zero abelianization and is nonidentity, while the centralizer of a free basis letter consists of its own powers (by free reduction). Every event controls a leaf of this iterated bracket. Thus the signed cut word is raw-nontrivial and every single-event contraction makes it raw-trivial. Folding the names to the one-rule tester preserves raw nonfilling by the based occurrence lift. In particular a bound on the number of uses retained by such projections cannot decide this part of the four-strand surface test. One obtains this ring from the circle bundle \(p:X\to\mathbb CP^\infty\) with first Chern class four times the generator. The fibre class survives modulo two, \(v\) pulls back from the base, and \(Sq^1u=0\) since the character lifts modulo four. Thus \(\widetilde H^*X\) splits as a Steenrod module into the line on \(u\), the positive even powers-of-\(v\) part \(v\mathbb F_2[v]\), and the part \(uv\mathbb F_2[v]\) in odd degrees greater than one. Here \(Sq^{2b}v^a=\binom ab v^{a+b}\), the same formula holds after multiplying by \(u\), and all odd squares vanish. The bottom-circle inclusion is split on cohomology as a module map, hence is injective on its sphere summand of Adams \(E_2\), in every filtration.

The dimension-shifting transfer of this principal circle bundle is a stable map \(\Sigma(\mathbb CP^\infty)_+\to X_+\). Its cohomology map is integration over the fibre, by the Pontryagin–Thom collapse and the framing of the vertical tangent. The class \(u\) restricts to the generator on that fibre, so the projection formula sends \(uv^a\) to the suspension of the base monomial of degree \(2a\). On the *reduced* suspension summand of the source, the transfer therefore projects cohomology exactly onto the odd summand above degree one. In particular the corresponding inclusion of Ext summands is induced by an actual stable map. Any \(d_2\) on a class from that summand has zero component on the bottom circle, by naturality. This excludes cancellation by classes coming from higher odd cells, which a bottom-cell calculation alone would miss. [Dimension-shifting transfer for the circle and its cyclic subgroups, Malkiewich §3](https://people.math.rochester.edu/faculty/doug/otherpapers/malkiewich.pdf#page=6)

The even summand has no filtration-one source in stem \(L\). To see this directly, extend the even module by a new class in degree \(L+1\). A square landing there from an even degree has odd index, and \(Sq^{2b+1}=Sq^1 Sq^{2b}\). It is enough to check \(Sq^1 v^{L/2}=0\) in the extension. Put \(k=L/2\) and \(c=v^{L/4}\), of degree \(k\). In degree \(L\) the lift of \(Sq^k c=v^{L/2}\) is unique. The Adem relations give
\[
      Sq^1 Sq^k=Sq^{k+1},\qquad
      Sq^2 Sq^{k-1}=Sq^{k+1}+Sq^k Sq^1 .
\]
The second leading coefficient is odd since \(4\mid k\). Both \(Sq^{k-1}c\) and \(Sq^1 c\) vanish below the top. Hence \(Sq^{k+1}c=0\). All possible top operations from the even module vanish and the extension splits.

On the bottom circle the nonzero reading is the suspended class \(h_j\). Adams's sphere differential is \(d_2h_j=h_0h_{j-1}^2\ne0\) for every \(j\ge4\). Its image on the bottom circle in \(X\) is nonzero by the split injection on \(E_2\). Every possible filtration-one source with the required reading is this bottom element plus a class from the higher odd summand. The latter differential has zero bottom component. The sum cannot be a cycle. This proves the claimed nonzero square for the full infinite lens space; in particular it also survives on the bottom of the suspended two-cell Moore space mapping to it. [Adams differential, Burklund–Xu, Theorem 1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.11869v2#S1.SS1)

### Characters and the published comparison

For every connected label \(K\) and dyadic \(L\ge16\), the natural surjection \(q_Y:A/2A\to T\) of [Response 165](#researcher-response-165) has kernel contained in the image of \(A[2]\). Indeed the intersection of the kernels of the mod-two reductions of all characters \(A\to C_4\) is precisely \((2A+A[2])/2A\). On the cyclic decomposition, a free summand or a summand of order divisible by four can map its generator to one, whereas a summand of order twice an odd integer can map it only to an even element. Any character is realized by \(K\to BC_4\). Suspending sends a square with odd character reading to the nonzero bottom square just proved. At \(m=15,31,63\) the Moore-space vanishing of Response 165 gives the opposite containment, proving the formula. For example \(A=\mathbb Z\oplus C_2\oplus C_4\oplus C_6\oplus C_8\) gives exactly three independent differences in degree 43.

If published insertion fails at one of these ranks and degrees, [Response 158](#researcher-response-158) produces a nonzero surface-null shell at one stationary puncture. A detecting character sends it to the prescribed comparison on \(BC_4\). Use the finite local Postnikov tester and the realization of maps by raw substitutions at the prescribed faces from [Response 163](#researcher-response-163); suspending the Postnikov comparison leaves this shell group unchanged. Conversely that tester lies in the class and its shell is raw-nonzero. This proves the uniform equivalence at each of the three degrees. The same equivalence holds at every dyadic \(L\ge16\) on the subclass with \(A[2]\subseteq 2A\).

There is an all-dyadic calculation allowing order-two factors as well. If the local type through the tested rank is \(B\pi\), and the image of \(A[2]\) in \(A/2A\) is spanned by classes of actual involutions of \(\pi\), the same formula holds for **every** dyadic \(L\ge16\). Each involution gives a map \(BC_2\to B\pi\); the bottom square of the suspended \(BC_2\) vanishes by Response 165. This gives exactly the opposite containment again. Examples include all finitely generated abelian groups with the stipulated finite local tester, and finite symmetric groups. For a group generated by involutions the shell group is zero, so published insertion reflects at every old boundary of this degree under the local reversibility hypotheses. This includes the symmetric-group examples at \(m=127\) independently of the order of a stem-126 Kervaire class. For a general connected label at that bottom dimension, possible further relations are confined to the image of \(A[2]\).

It solves the Adem equations on extensions of the actual lens-space module and quotients the freedom in lifting a base class to the top degree. At \(L=16,32,64,128\) it finds two primary extension directions in the full degree range, with exactly one on the bottom and the other supported on higher odd degrees. At \(L=16\) the latter has top readings from degrees 9 and 13. ### The two Adams groups that control the bound

Let \(t\) be the displayed upper bound minus \(d\), and let \(Z\) be the \((d+t)\)-skeleton of a model of \(K(C_q,d)\) starting with the Moore complex \(M=S^d\cup_q e^{d+1}\). Write \(x\) for the suspended bottom generator in \(\pi_m(\Sigma^n Z)\). If \([x,x]=0\), extend the two bottom maps over \(S^m\times S^m\) and take the Hopf construction of [Response 165](#the-bottom-square-for-a-projective-label). Desuspending stably gives a map \(S^{d+L-1}\to Z\) with nonzero \(Sq^L\) on the degree-\(d\) class of its cone. Its mod-two Hurewicz image vanishes by dimension. The top reading therefore specifies a nonzero Adams filtration-one extension, represented by a cycle in bidegree \((1,d+L)\). Throughout write \((s,b)\) for filtration and **internal degree**, with stem \(b-s\).

On a sphere in degree \(d+r\), filtration one in that bidegree is possible only if \(L-r\) is a power of two. In the non-dyadic row there is no such offset \(0\le r\le t\). Filter the mod-two cohomology module by degree and use the Ext exact sequences. Its associated quotients are sums of sphere modules in precisely this range. The filtration-one group vanishes, so the supposed extension cannot occur.

In the dyadic rows put \(L=2^j\), \(j\ge4\). On \(M\) the degree-\(d\) and degree-\((d+1)\) cohomology lines split as Steenrod modules: the bottom character lifts mod four and thus has \(Sq^1=0\). The inclusion \(M\to Z\) induces a surjection in mod-two cohomology. Indeed the universal degree-\(d\) mod-four class restricts to the fundamental one on \(M\); the integral Bockstein of that class restricts to the generator of \(H^{d+1}(M;\mathbb Z)=C_4\), which reduces nontrivially mod two. Hence the kernel of this cohomology surjection has support only at offsets \(2\le r\le t\).

In bidegree \((1,d+L)\) the sphere on the bottom contributes \(h_j\) and all offsets \(1\le r\le t\) contribute zero. The Ext exact sequence therefore shows that **every** filtration-one candidate on \(Z\) is in the image of the bottom sphere. It remains to check that its differential stays nonzero. In bidegree \((3,d+L+1)\) the bottom class \(h_0h_{j-1}^2\) is nonzero on \(M\) by the module splitting. The map from \(M\) to \(Z\) is injective on Ext in this bidegree if the cohomology kernel above has zero Ext in \((2,d+L+1)\). At offset \(r\) that possible relation has internal degree \(L+1-r\) in sphere Ext. The sphere 2-line has basis \(h_a h_b\) with \(a\le b\) and \(b\ne a+1\), of internal degree \(2^a+2^b\). Naturality now carries the sphere differential \(d_2h_j=h_0h_{j-1}^2\ne0\) to a nonzero differential on \(Z\). There is no cycle with the required bottom reading. This calculation proves \([x,x]\ne0\). The first additional offset beyond the bound has a possible 2-line relation; its degree alone does not determine its effect. ## Researcher Response 172

**There is a sharp path-growth threshold for the degree-four recognition problem of Response 169.** Count the *unquotiented* paths from \(s\) to \(t\) of length at most \(N\). If this count is \(O(N)\), reflection through dimension four is decidable uniformly in the graph, the path equations and the finite erasure list \(D\). On one fixed graph with count \(\Theta(N^2)\), it is \(\Pi^0_2\)-complete even with a single fixed erasure. On that graph one fixed presentation also has a \(\Sigma^0_1\)-complete individual half-twist test. In contrast, **all-dimensional reflection is decidable throughout this entire path-presentation family**, with no growth bound. It holds exactly when the graph has no path from \(s\) to \(t\) and the list of path equations is empty. The family here uses the round-trip declarations specified in [Response 169](#researcher-response-169).

### Linear growth gives finitely many one-counter tests

Trim the graph to edges and vertices on completed paths for the degree-four question. A replacement occurring in a completed path uses two parallel subpaths, so either side of that replacement lies in the trim. In the trim, linear growth is equivalent to two conditions. Each cyclic strongly connected component is a simple directed cycle, and each successful route in the condensation visits at most one cyclic component. An internal branch in a strongly connected component gives two return words based at the branch with distinct first edges and no internal return to that vertex. Their concatenations have exponential growth. Two cyclic components in series give independently pumpable lap counts and at least quadratic growth. Conversely, under the two conditions the completed paths decompose uniquely into finitely many isolated paths and finitely many rays \((q,k)\), \(k\ge0\). Record the edges between components, the entry and exit vertices, and the unique segment of less than one lap between them. The only remaining choice is the number of full laps. This proves the growth criterion and computes the decomposition.

For an equation \(u=v:i\to j\), apply the same decomposition to the two exterior paths \(p:s\to i\) and \(z:j\to t\). For each pair of exterior routes, first take zero optional laps and record the endpoints \(puz,pvz\) of the replacement in completed-path coordinates. If neither exterior route has a cycle, this is a single exact edge. Otherwise it gives precisely the translated edges
\[
                    (q,a+h)\ \longleftrightarrow\ (r,b+h)\qquad(h\ge0).
\]
Each extra lap is on the same cycle on both sides since it belongs to the unchanged exterior. If both exterior routes admit a lap, their cycle is the same and the two counts add. This also covers identity subpaths and equations that change the route. These finite schemes generate exactly the path congruence. An individual erasure query is now finite-control one-counter reachability. In each orientation pop the specified input count, test zero for an exact edge, then push the output count, using private intermediate states. The balanced push/pop decision in [round-1 Response 49](../answered/semistrict-surface-conservativity-2026-11-24.md#researcher-response-49) decides each such query.

To decide coverage, give a translated edge the signed weight \(b-a\) on the finite graph of ray states. In a component in which all closed walks have weight zero, choose a vertex potential by integrating the weights. Height minus potential is invariant under all translated edges there. The list \(D\) and the ends of exact edges supply only finitely many such invariant values. A sufficiently high point of a ray in this component cannot reach any of them, so coverage fails. In every other component and at *each* of its states \(q\), transport a nonzero closed walk along a connecting path and reverse it if needed to get weight \(d>0\). A spanning tree and its first inconsistent edge find the walk effectively. Let \(a\) be the maximum of zero and the input threshold of each step minus the displacement accumulated before it. At every \(k\ge a\) the walk realizes \((q,k)\sim(q,k+d)\). It therefore suffices to test heights \(0\le k<a+d\) on this ray, and each isolated path. This proves the degree-four decision by the coverage and strand-erasure theorem of Response 169, even when the path category has infinitely many morphisms.

### Quadratic growth can encode totality on a fixed graph

Take two internal vertices with one unary loop each, labelled \(a,b\), an opening \(l\) at the first, a closing \(r\) at the second, and a bridge edge for each control state \(q\) of a finite program. All completed paths are uniquely
\[
                            l\,a^i\,q\,b^j\,r .
\]
For \(N\ge3\) there are \(|Q|\binom{N-1}{2}\) of length at most \(N\). A left increment with successor \(p\) gives \(q=ap\). A left decrement with positive successor \(p\) and zero successor \(z\) gives \(aq=p\) and \(lq=lz\). The right instructions use \(q=pb\), or \(qb=p\) and \(qr=zr\). Unconditional jumps use \(q=p\). A bulk increment uses a corresponding power of the loop. Send every halt to the state \(H\). There use \(aH=H\) and \(lHb=lH\), so even an arbitrary starting configuration at \(H\) reaches the sole terminal \(lHr\). All equations are typed. Each matched factor contains the unique bridge, and an endpoint gate tests exactly the indicated zero counter. Hence the oriented replacements are precisely machine execution. In a deterministic transition graph the basin of a terminal is closed in both directions along every edge, and every vertex of the basin is connected to the terminal by its run. Thus signed equation reachability of \(lHr\) is exactly termination, at every completed path.

Here is a fixed-control reduction proving the claimed degree, including for starting configurations inside the simulation. For a machine index \(e\), use a register program with persistent input \(x\) and clock \(t\). At each main entry set a parameter register to \(e\), initialize work registers, and compute whether machine \(e\) halts on \(x\) within \(t\) steps. On success go to \(H\), otherwise increment \(t\) and repeat. This is a single bounded simulation program with a varying constant. For example, use a standard primitive recursive encoding of configurations and iterate the primitive recursive single-step function exactly \(t\) times, with halting states stationary. Primitive recursive subroutines compile to finite nested counted loops by induction on composition and primitive recursion, using a fresh decreasing counter for each loop bound. They preserve the two persistent inputs at ordinary main entries. From *any* internal instruction a bounded block exits in finite time even with arbitrary register contents. Induct on its loop nesting, since the remaining body leaves the enclosing remaining-iteration counter untouched except for its scheduled decrement. Thus an arbitrary start either halts or reaches a fresh main entry with some \(x,t\). Totality of \(e\) then suffices for every start to halt. A divergent input gives a divergent run from a main entry with that input and clock zero.

For clarity, the number of bridge states can be fixed before choosing \(e\). Encode the finitely many registers as prime exponents of a positive first counter, using a second counter for scratch. At each register-instruction entry empty the scratch and replace zero in the first counter by one. Increment of a register multiplies the first counter by its fixed prime: consume its units into scratch in batches of that prime and transfer back. A conditional decrement divides by the prime with a remainder in finite control. On zero remainder transfer the quotient back and take the positive branch; otherwise restore the original number by multiplying the quotient back and adding the remainder, and take the zero branch. Other prime factors never affect a test. To load \(e\), clear its register by conditional decrements, then multiply by its fixed prime to the power \(e\), using a single bulk addition of that constant to scratch per consumed unit. This changes one right-hand path length in the presentation while leaving its control graph fixed. Each arithmetic phase drains a source counter, with a finite transfer or remainder correction before the next phase. From an arbitrary internal instruction it reaches an instruction entry or halt in finite time. At a normalized entry the encoding then simulates exactly. This proves the reduction from totality, and the upper bound enumerates paths and finite signed equation derivations. Taking the sole erasure \(lHr\) gives the claimed \(\Pi^0_2\)-completeness. Fixing \(e\) to be a universal machine instead gives a computable reduction from its halting set to the half twist on two copies of an encoded initial path. Membership of this individual comparison is computably enumerable by Response 169. [The distinction between total and uniformly bounded mortality, §5](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol228-fscd2022/LIPIcs.FSCD.2022.16/LIPIcs.FSCD.2022.16.pdf#page=11)

### Reflection in all dimensions on the same presentations

If there is a completed path, its closed 2-writing is a positive bubble at the empty wire. Response 4 excludes all-dimensional reflection regardless of the higher equations. If there is any path equation, take its raw round trip \(h\) at the written 2-cell \(u\). The prescribed 4-declarations include \(1_u\to h\) and \(h\to1_u\). Their composite is a positive 4-bubble at \(1_u\), so the same obstruction applies in degree six since there are no 6-generators. This argument uses the original graph, including equations outside the trim. With neither a completed path nor any equation there are no erasures or higher declarations. Every connected floating component on this unary planar base would be a completed path. The 2-computad criterion therefore gives reflection in every dimension. In particular, when there is no completed path but at least one equation, degree four always reflects, and the first failure is in degree five or six. ### Delooping the character once

Write \(X_e=K(C_2,e)\) and \(u_e\) for its mod-two fundamental class. Let \(b\) be the bottom generator of \(\Sigma^n X_d\). If \([b,b]=0\), take an extension of the two copies of \(b\) over \(S^m\times S^m\) and its Hopf construction \(f:S^{2m+1}\to\Sigma^{n+1}X_d\). Postcompose with \(\Sigma^n e\), where \(e:\Sigma X_d\to X_{d+1}\) represents the suspension of \(u_d\). The composite \(f'\) is the Hopf construction of the extension postcomposed with \(\Sigma^{n-1}e\), and both its axes still pair to one with the bottom class.

**The mod-two Hurewicz image of \(f'\) is zero, even when the Hurewicz image of \(f\) is unknown.** In degree \(d+L\) of \(X_{d+1}\), products of positive classes pull back to zero on the suspension \(\Sigma X_d\). The polynomial generators in this degree are positive Steenrod operations on \(u_{d+1}\), by Serre's description of the cohomology. They pull back along \(e\) to the same operations on \(\Sigma u_d\). After the remaining suspensions the bottom class pulls back to zero on the source sphere of \(f\) by degree, so every such operation also pulls back to zero. These exhaust the cohomology in question. The relative top class therefore injects in the cone of \(f'\). The relative disk product calculation of [Response 165](#the-bottom-square-for-a-projective-label) gives \(Sq^L c=c^2\ne0\) on the extension \(c\) of \(\Sigma^n u_{d+1}\). ### An Adem relation with a uniform instability bound

Write \(B=L-r\), a positive multiple of \(2r\). In the Steenrod algebra, \(Sq^L\) is a sum of words \(Sq^a Sq^b Sq^I\) with \(a>0\) and \(b-|I|\ge L-2r+1\). Here \(|I|\) is the total degree of the remaining word. To construct the relation, begin with \(Sq^{B+h}Sq^I\) at \(h=r\), \(I\) empty. Keep \(1\le h\le r\) and \(|I|=r-h\). Set \(a=2^{v_2(h)}\), \(b=B+h-a\). In the Adem relation for \(Sq^a Sq^b\), the coefficient of \(Sq^{B+h}\) is one because \(2a\mid b\) and \(\binom{b-1}{a}\) is odd. Solve for that term. Retain \(Sq^a Sq^b Sq^I\), and recurse on each other term \(Sq^{B+h-j}Sq^j Sq^I\) with nonzero coefficient, where \(1\le j\le a/2<h\). The recursion terminates. Every retained term has
\[
                b-|I|=L-2r+2h-a\ \ge\ L-2r+1 .
\]
If \(n\ge2r\), then \(d+1=L-n\le L-2r\). In every retained term, instability kills \(Sq^b Sq^I u_{d+1}\) on the unsuspended label. Stability and restriction below the new cell kill \(Sq^b Sq^I c\) in the cone: its degree is below the top because \(a>0\). Consequently \(Sq^L c=0\), contradicting the Hopf construction. This proves the bottom square is nonzero on \(\Sigma^n X_d\).

### The degree-12 comparison

For \(d=2\), write \(L=kr\), with odd \(k\ge3\). Then \(L-2r=(k-2)r\ge4\) except at \(L=6\). Thus \(n=L-3\ge2r\) in every other case. At \(L=6\), use the original Hopf construction over \(X_2\) directly. Write \(u=u_2\), \(v=Sq^1u\), \(w=Sq^2v\). The full degree-seven cohomology of \(X_2\) has basis \(u^2v,uw\). By Cartan,
\[
 Sq^1(u^3)=u^2v,\qquad Sq^2(uv)=u^2v+uw .
\]
Both pull back to zero on the stable sphere, so the top class again injects. But \(Sq^6=Sq^2Sq^4+Sq^1Sq^4Sq^1\), and \(Sq^4\) kills both \(u\) and \(v\) by instability. Each inner vanishing occurs below the new cell. This excludes a zero bottom square also at \(n=3,m=5\).

Finally, each nonzero class of \(A/2A\) has a character to \(C_2\) taking value one. Universal coefficients realize it by a map \(K\to X_d\). Naturality takes its square to the nonzero one above, proving injectivity. Surjectivity is [Response 163](#researcher-response-163). The finite tester and raw substitution realizing the character on the local \(i\)-types are those of Responses 158 and 163. Their suspended Postnikov comparisons preserve \(\pi_{i+1}\). Hence a nonzero surface-null difference at a puncture transports a filler to the single comparison, and a filler there is itself a counterexample. The calculation decides the raw group and which published comparison suffices. Existence of that published filler remains open.

**Reproduce.** Run `python3 -B tools/semistrict_surface_character_squares.py --through 64`. It normalizes each recursive certificate independently in the admissible Steenrod basis and checks the bound for every summand. It also computes the spherical upper bound and the possible new-cell readings directly on the Serre polynomial basis of \(X_2\), verifying the ordinary Adem relations on the base at the same time. For this calculation, \(g_j\) has degree \(2^j+1\), beginning with \(g_0=u\) and \(g_{j+1}=Sq^{2^j}g_j\). Apart from the identity, this generator operation and the top square, the only nonzero operation is \(Sq^1g_j=g_{j-1}^2\) for \(j\ge2\). One can verify the action by evaluating primitives on \(xy\) over \(BC_2\times BC_2\): \(g_j\) maps to \(x^{2^j}y+xy^{2^j}\) for \(j\ge1\). Each positive degree has at most one primitive basis vector in the polynomial Hopf algebra (a power of two of a primitive generator), and each has nonzero image. Cartan on the two polynomial variables gives the stated action. The two direct tests both exclude a vanishing square at lengths 6, 10, 12, 14, 20, 24, 26, 40, 48, 56 and 60 through 64. The delooping argument supplies every other non-power in this range and at arbitrary length for \(d=2\). Use `--certificate 12` to print a specific relation, or run `python3 -B tools/semistrict_surface_bottom_squares.py --rank 3 --bottom 5 --orders 0 2 4` for the exact degree-12 group. ## Researcher Response 174

**Published insertion reflects at every old boundary in degree \(2m+1\) at stationary rank two when the reversible local type is \(K(G,m-2)\), for every odd \(m\ge3\) and finitely generated abelian \(G\).** At \(m=5\) this resolves degree 11 even for an infinite cyclic bottom group. More generally let \(L=m+1\), \(d=m-n\ge1\), \(i=2m-2\), with rank \(n\ge2\) and the connectivity and reversibility assumptions of [Response 153](#researcher-response-153). Factor \(L=2^{4a+b}u\) with \(u\) odd and \(0\le b<4\), and put \(\rho(L)=8a+2^b\). The same reflection result holds in degree \(n+2m-1\) for local \(i\)-type \(P_iK(G,d)\) whenever \(n\le\rho(L)\). For example \(L=16\) allows all stationary ranks two through nine.

### A finite label that kills the square on an integral generator

Choose \(n-1\) orthonormal tangent fields on \(S^m\). The Hurwitz–Radon construction supplies them in precisely the indicated range. Let \(V\) be their orthogonal complement in the tangent bundle, of rank \(d+1\), and \(E=S(V)\) its unit sphere bundle. The fibre \(S^d\to E\) generates \(H_d E=\mathbb Z\): over the two-cell structure of \(S^m\), one starts with the fibre and attaches cells in degrees \(m\) and \(m+d\), both above \(d+1\). This follows by trivializing over the base disk and attaching \(D^m\times S^d\) along its boundary, using the zero and top cells of the fibre. At rank two, multiplication by \(i\) on \(\mathbb C^{L/2}\) supplies the field. The resulting \(E\) is the space of orthonormal complex two-frames, in particular \(SU(3)\) for \(m=5\). [Adams, *Vector fields on spheres*, introduction and Theorem 1.1](https://www.math.ens.psl.eu/~benoist/refs/Adams.pdf)

Let \(x:S^m\to\Sigma^n E\) be the suspended fibre. To prove \([x,x]=0\), collapse the complement of a tubular neighbourhood of the diagonal in \(S^m\times S^m\) onto the Thom basepoint. Its normal bundle is \(TS^m\). Follow this collapse by
\[
 \mathrm{Th}(TS^m)\simeq\Sigma^{n-1}\mathrm{Th}(V)
       \longrightarrow\Sigma^n E_+\longrightarrow\Sigma^n E.
\]
The middle arrow suspends the connecting map of the disk/sphere bundle cofibration \(E_+\to D(V)_+\to\mathrm{Th}(V)\). On a single Thom fibre it is the suspension of the inclusion of the unit sphere, up to sign, by naturality for \((D^{d+1},S^d)\). Each coordinate axis meets the diagonal transversely once. Its restriction under collapse consequently has degree one up to sign onto the normal fibre: fixing the other coordinate identifies the normal derivative with \(I\) or \(-I\). Thus the composite extends the two fibre classes, up to independent signs, over the product. Translating basepoints along paths gives the same Whitehead vanishing, since the suspended target is simply connected. This proves the claim in the actual unstable group \(\pi_{2m-1}(\Sigma^n E)\).

Consequently, in any label whose bottom homology modulo two is generated by images of these fibre classes under local maps from \(E\), all the generators of the obstruction group in [Response 163](#researcher-response-163) vanish. For a local \(K(G,d)\), each element of \(G\) is realized by such a map: choose the homomorphism from \(H_d E\) and lift it by universal coefficients. The same reasoning works on local \(i\)-types by the suspended Postnikov connectivity of Response 158. More generally, it suffices that bottom homology modulo two be generated by spherical classes of the local label and that \(\pi_{m-1}K=\pi_{m+d-1}K=0\) in the chosen component. Extend each representing fibre map over the two remaining cells of \(E\) using these two groups. These criteria give \(T_{n,i}=0\), hence actual published reflection by the one-puncture reduction. The finite bundle label itself has a reversible presentation through \(i\): realize its fibre first, then its two attaching spheres at their prescribed faces and complete reversibility at each stage as in [Response 158](#researcher-response-158). Its top cell has dimension \(m+d\le i\). Local inverse completions preserve the required suspended group.

### A sharp dimension cutoff in stationary rank two

Take \(L\equiv2\pmod4\), \(L\ge6\), \(n=2\), \(d=L-3\). If the local label admits a CW model through its \(i\)-type of dimension at most \(2d+1\), then \(T_{2,i}\cong H_d(K)/2H_d(K)\). At dimension **\(2d+2\)** the bundle just constructed has \(H_d=\mathbb Z\) and \(T_{2,i}=0\). Thus the cutoff is exact for a statement uniform in all such labels. In degree 11 it is seven versus eight; in degree 19 it is fifteen versus sixteen. The local sphere \(S^d\) and the bundle have identical bottom homology and different obstruction groups in each case.

For the nonvanishing proof, if a square with a nonzero character were zero, the product extension would give the stable Hopf map of Response 173, followed by the character to \(X_d=K(C_2,d)\). Its domain stem is \(d+L-1=2d+2\). Its mod-two Hurewicz image vanishes by the dimension bound on its source **label**, so the relative top class injects in the cone over the character target. Write \(u=u_d\). The Adem identity is
\[
             Sq^L=Sq^2Sq^{L-2}+Sq^1Sq^{L-2}Sq^1 .
\]
The first inner operation vanishes on \(u\). In the second, \(Sq^{L-2}Sq^1u=(Sq^1u)^2=Sq^1(u\,Sq^1u)\) by instability and Cartan. Lift the latter product as a class from the old base, after suspension, below the new cell. Restriction is an isomorphism in the degrees in question, using the zero Hurewicz image at the degree immediately below the top. The outer \(Sq^1\) now kills the inner class by \(Sq^1Sq^1=0\). This contradicts the top reading of the Hopf construction. All nonzero mod-two coordinates are thus detected. For a single finite test **within the bounded family**, use the \((2d+1)\)-skeleton of \(X_d\), completed through \(i\) as in Response 171. Character maps out of the bounded model land in this skeleton by cellular approximation. The existence of a published filler at this nonzero comparison is still open.

There is a rank improvement for every non-power-of-two length in [Response 173](#researcher-response-173). With \(r=2^{v_2(L)}\), **\(n\ge2r-1\)** now suffices without any label dimension bound. At equality the once-delooped fundamental class has degree \(L-2r+1\). In the recursive Adem proof only terms attaining the lower excess bound need a new argument. Equality \(2h-a=1\) forces \(h=a=1\). This value of \(h\) is reached only from \(h=2\) with \(j=1\), since a step subtracts at most half the current value and the initial \(r\) is even. Thus the tail begins with \(Sq^1\), and the outer operation is also \(Sq^1\). The middle operation on the label is the top square of \(Sq^1 z\), equal to \(Sq^1(z\,Sq^1z)\). The preceding lift argument kills that term in the cone. The once-delooped Hurewicz image is zero by Response 173. In particular, for \(L\equiv2\pmod4\), the mod-two character square is zero in rank two and nonzero at every allowable rank at least three. For higher ranks the one-comparison result applies to all labels, and at rank two the bundle gives the stated positive reflection cases.

**Reproduce.** Run `python3 -B tools/semistrict_surface_frame_labels.py`. The solver constructs actual signed permutation matrices representing the tangent fields from complex, quaternionic and octonionic sizes and real Clifford periodicity. It checks the negative square of each matrix and pairwise anticommutation on every basis vector at eleven ambient dimensions through 384, including non-powers of two. Skew orthogonal matrices with these identities give orthonormal vectors \(A_jv\) perpendicular to each unit vector \(v\). Use `--rank 2 --bottom 5` for the degree-11 bundle and dimension cutoff, or `--rank 9 --bottom 15` for the eight-field example. Run `python3 -B tools/semistrict_surface_character_squares.py --through 64` for the equality terms in the independent Adem normalization, and `python3 -B tools/semistrict_surface_bottom_squares.py --rank 3 --bottom 9 --orders 0 2 4` for three independent degree-20 classes. The Thom collapse and prescribed-boundary implications are proved above. ## Researcher Response 175

**At stationary rank two, the relations among all bottom Whitehead squares are computable from one characteristic number at each stable spherical homology class when \(m\equiv1\pmod4\), \(m\ge5\).** This includes arbitrary higher attaching maps in the reversible presentations of [Response 153](#researcher-response-153). In old degree 11, every binary linear subspace occurs as the full set of raw relations among named squares on a finite presentation. A single old comparison tests published insertion on the entire family of signed attaching matrices constructed below, with arbitrarily many generators, relations and integer coefficients.

Put \(d=m-2\), \(N=2d+2\), \(Y=\Sigma^2K\), and \(A=H_d(K;\mathbb Z)\), with \(Y\) \((m-1)\)-connected as before. Write \(h_2\) for the mod-two stable Hurewicz map. The exact one-puncture group is
\[
 T_{2,2m-2}(Y)=(A/2A)/\operatorname{im}\lambda_K,\qquad
 \langle c,\lambda_K(f)\rangle
     =\langle c\smile Sq^2c,h_2(f)\rangle ,
 \quad f\in\pi_N^S K,\quad c\in H^d(K;\mathbb F_2).
\]
Here the cohomology characters are exactly the dual of \(A/2A\), by connectivity and universal coefficients. The right-hand pairing is linear in \(c\) on the spherical image. In particular, on a closed connected stably framed label of dimension \(N\) there is at most one independent relation; its coordinates are the characteristic numbers on the mod-two fundamental class. The Pontryagin–Thom map of a stable normal framing represents that class in stable homotopy. When the quotient is zero this proves published reflection at every written boundary in degree \(2d+5\). [Miller, the stable fundamental class in the Pontryagin–Thom construction](https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/papers/sb-final.pdf)

### Why the characteristic number gives every relation

For odd \(m\), the exact sequence of the James pair in [Response 163](#researcher-response-163) maps \(\pi_{2m+1}\Sigma Y\) to \(A\otimes A\) by the second Hopf invariant \(H\), followed by \(x\otimes y\mapsto[x,y]\). Indeed the relative Hurewicz map projects onto length two, where the second James–Hopf map sends the two-letter word to its smash. The image of \(H\) is invariant under swapping tensor factors: the second reading of the following bracket is \(1-\tau\) on tensors by Response 163. On the invariant tensors quotient by all norms \(t+\tau t\). The natural map from \(A/2A\) sending \(x\) to \(x\otimes x\) in this quotient is an isomorphism. In a cyclic decomposition the paired off-diagonal coordinates are norms, and a diagonal has exactly its quotient by doubling. The bracket kills every norm, by odd-dimensional skew symmetry. Its map on this quotient is exactly the square map to \(T\).

The map \(H\) modulo norms factors through stable homotopy. Indeed the first suspension on \(\pi_{2m+1}\Sigma Y\) is onto, with kernel generated by the Whitehead products of the suspended bottom classes, again by the James pair. All later suspensions are isomorphisms in this stem. The adjoint of each such product has the graded commutator of the two degree-\(m\) elements in length two; since \(m\) is odd its Hopf tensor is a norm, with consistent orientations. This gives a natural map \(\pi_N^S K\to A/2A\) with image precisely the relations, by exactness. Evaluation on a character reduces its calculation to \(X=K(C_2,d)\) and the fundamental class \(u\).

On \(X\) this map vanishes on \(\ker h_2\). Represent a stable class there by \(f:S^{2m+1}\to\Sigma^3 X\). Its cone has an injective new top cohomology class. By Boardman–Steer's cone diagonal formula the square of the lifted bottom class is its Hopf tensor evaluated on \(u\otimes u\), times that top class. But the cone calculation in [Response 174](#a-sharp-dimension-cutoff-in-stationary-rank-two) kills this square using \(Sq^{m+1}=Sq^2 Sq^{m-1}+Sq^1 Sq^{m-1} Sq^1\) and \((Sq^1u)^2=Sq^1(u Sq^1u)\). This argument uses only the zero Hurewicz image of this particular \(f\). [Boardman and Steer, Theorem 5.14 and Corollary 5.15](https://www.e-periodica.ch/cntmng?pid=com-001%3A1967%3A42%3A%3A15#page=25)

In degree \(N\) of \(X\), every single Serre polynomial generator is a positive operation on \(u\), hence pairs to zero with spherical homology. Three positive factors already exceed \(N\). The only possible two-factor monomials are \(u Sq^2u\) and \((Sq^1u)^2\); the latter is itself hit by \(Sq^1\). Thus the spherical image has dimension at most one, with only the first product able to detect it. On the other hand the square on the bottom generator of \(\Sigma^2 X\) vanishes by the sphere-bundle construction of Response 174. The exact sequence therefore makes the stable Hopf map onto \(C_2\). Its factor through spherical homology must be the unique nonzero functional there, namely evaluation on \(u Sq^2u\). Applying every character proves the displayed formula, including its asserted linearity. For a finite simplicial label the spherical image can in principle be computed by suspending into the stable range, taking simplicial representatives of homotopy generators, and pushing forward their fundamental cycles. The matrix family below has a direct calculation. [Serre, polynomial generators of Eilenberg–MacLane cohomology](https://www.college-de-france.fr/media/jean-pierre-serre/UPL1337078477518797719_Serre_Cohomologie_mod_2_des_complexes_d_Eilenberg_MacLane.pdf) · [Filakovský–Franek–Wagner–Zhechev, Theorem A](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.00380)

### Realizing and testing arbitrary binary relations

Let \(E\) be Response 174's complex two-frame bundle over \(S^m\), with fibre \(S^d\). Write \(W\) for its skeleton before the top disk and \(g:S^{N-1}\to W\) for the attaching map. Then
\[
                     \Sigma^2g= [x,x]\ne0\quad\text{in }\pi_{2m-1}\Sigma^2W,
\]
up to orientation, with \(x\) the bottom generator. In fact \(E\) is stably parallelizable: for its bundle projection \(p\), \(TE\oplus1\cong p^*(TS^m\oplus V)\), and \(V\oplus1\cong TS^m\) is stably trivial. The stable fundamental class splits the top cell off stably, so \(g\) is stably null. Freudenthal therefore places \(\Sigma^2g\) in the subgroup generated by the single square. That square survives on \(W\) by the sharp dimension bound in Response 174 and dies on \(E\), so the attaching map is its nonzero generator.

Fix an integer matrix \(M\) with \(b\) columns. Start from \(\bigvee_{j=1}^b W_j\); for each row attach an \(N\)-disk by \(\sum_j M_{ij}g_j\) using the wedge inclusions. Complete the finite local presentation through \(i=N\) as in Response 158. After double suspension the squares on the wedge are independent by retraction to its factors. Each new disk attaches by the indicated binary sum of them. These are all relations: relative Hurewicz for the pair obtained by attaching the \(2m\)-disks gives a free relative group on the disks in degree \(2m\), and its boundary gives exactly the kernel in degree \(2m-1\). Thus \(T\cong\mathbb F_2^b/\mathrm{rows}(M\bmod2)\). For instance, rows \((1,1,0),(0,1,1)\) make all three squares equal and nonzero. With the single row \((1,1,1)\) the three squares are nonzero, pairwise distinct, and sum to zero. Both examples already occur in degree 11.

Use the **one-column matrix \((2)\)** and compare its bottom square to zero. Its raw difference survives. A failed boundary anywhere in this family gives a surface-null nonzero vector in the quotient at one puncture. Choose a binary character annihilating the rows and evaluating to one on that vector. Fold the selected \(W_j\) identically onto the tester skeleton, and collapse the others to its basepoint. On each attaching sphere the image is an *integer* multiple \(k_i g\) with \(k_i\) even. The tester disk supplies the extension of relative degree \(k_i/2\), also for negative coefficients. The induced local map gives a raw substitution through the tested faces by Response 158 and carries the hypothesized filler to the test. Conversely that test is a member of the family. Hence its published nonfilling is equivalent to reflection throughout the signed-matrix family in the specified degree. Its published status remains open.

**Reproduce.** Run `python3 -B tools/semistrict_surface_framed_relations.py`. The solver enumerates Serre monomials, evaluates Steenrod squares by Adem reduction, instability and Cartan, and checks that \(u Sq^2u\) spans the quotient by positive operations in degree \(2d+2\) for \(d=3,7,\ldots,31\). It also checks 5,832 individual comparisons for signed two-row matrices against direct enumeration of attaching relations, including the integral disk degrees for every separating fold. Use `--degree 3 --columns 3 --row 1 1 0 --row 0 1 1 --shell 1 0 0` for the nonzero common square, or change the shell to `1 0 1` for a raw filler. ## Researcher Response 176

**For the ordinary join \(J\), a finite 3-computad fails at the two empty 2-ends of a vertex in any specified degree \(d\ge5\) exactly when there is a positive 3-program from those ends back to themselves. In that case it fails there in *every* degree \(d\ge5\).** The test is P-complete for scalar-rule presentations and \(\Sigma^0_1\)-complete for general finite 3-computads, already with one generating edge in the latter case. Moreover, every finite ordinary computad has finite extensions whose exact spectrum of joined failure is any prescribed tail \(h+1,h+2,\ldots\) with \(h\ge\max(3,\dim X)\). Thus even when a specified subcomputad forces all-dimensional failure in every finite extension, the first failure of the extension can be postponed arbitrarily far.

### A split subgroup of the kernel at twice the weight

Start with one raw generating \(m\)-scalar at the iterated identity of a vertex, \(m\ge3\). Write \(F_k=\operatorname{Conf}_k(\mathbb R^m)\) for the configuration of \(k\) **named** points, and \(U_k=F_k/S_k\). At grouped written poles the weight-\(k\) space of raw \(m\)-cells is \(U_k\). For \(j\ge2\) the cover induces an isomorphism on \(\pi_j\). A based \(j\)-sphere represents an old comparison of degree \(d=m+j+1\), with a raw filler precisely for the zero class. This calculation applies at the written faces by the fixed-hom comparison. The comparison sends this raw groupoid into the invertible cells of the surface hom, since it preserves raw inverses and their higher witnesses. A class mapping to zero there has a surface filler at the indicated old boundary. [Raw scalar hom and boundary fits](#the-directed-test-at-two-equal-occurrences) · [Surface group test above the generating dimension](../answered/semistrict-surface-conservativity-2026-11-24.md#the-ordinary-surface-test-above-the-generating-dimension)

Put a grouped row \(w\) of \(k\) occurrences in each of two disjoint disks. Let \(i_1:F_k\to F_{2k}\) move the first block and keep the second fixed. In the unordered component at these ends the suspended raw exchange \(g=E_{m-2}(w,w)\) interchanges the blocks. It is definitionally the identity in \(J\) by the generic calculation on two scalar variables, substituting \(w\) in both slots. For \(v\in\pi_j F_k\) define
\[
               \delta(v)=(i_1)_*v-g_* (i_1)_*v\quad\in\pi_j U_{2k},
\]
where \(g_*\) denotes basepoint transport around the loop. Its surface value is zero by naturality of that transport. Lift both summands to the named cover and forget the second block. This recovers \(v\) on the first summand since moving inside the first disk induces the identity up to the chosen basepoint transport. On the second summand it reads the stationary block, hence zero. Indeed the lift of \(g\) ends at a labelling exchanging the two sets of names. Any basepoint path used to return from that reading still transports zero to zero. This gives a left inverse to \(\delta\) and embeds the *whole* group \(\pi_j F_k\) as a split subgroup of the raw group contained in the comparison kernel. In particular a torsion class has its original order in the kernel. No choice of a filling disk for a nontrivial raw exchange entered the construction. [Exchange on substituted blocks](#researcher-response-4)

Consequently the exact failed degrees on this pure scalar context are \(m+2\) and the degrees \(m+j+1\), \(j\ge2\), for which
\[
         \pi_j\big(S^{1+\ell(m-2)}\big)\ne0
                 \qquad\text{for some }\ell\ge1,\quad 1+\ell(m-2)\le j .
\]
For necessity in the higher degrees, forgetting the last named point is a fibration with a section (place the new point farther out than all the given points). Its fibre is a wedge of \((m-1)\)-spheres. Induct on the number of points and use Hilton's decomposition of the wedge groups. A basic word of length \(\ell\) contributes a sphere of the displayed dimension. If every indicated group vanishes, all the raw sphere differences vanish at every weight. For sufficiency two wedge letters already have a basic word of each length, for example successive brackets of one letter with the other. The fibre at the third point thus contains every required summand and injects into \(\pi_j F_3\) by the section. Apply \(\delta\), using at most six occurrences. Degree \(m+2\) itself uses the two-copy permutation. Through degree \(m+1\) point-only faces fit, all scalar counts have representatives, and each fixed-count configuration is connected, giving reflection by strict soundness. [Fadell–Neuwirth fibrations](https://doi.org/10.7146/math.scand.a-10517) · [Hilton's sphere summands](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms/s1-30.2.154) · [Low-degree scalar calculation](#researcher-response-78)

For \(m=3\) the sphere dimensions \(1+\ell(m-2)\) exhaust all \(j\ge2\). At each degree the identity class on the sphere of that dimension already gives the requisite nonzero element. ### Prescribing the entire tail of failures over an arbitrary finite context

Here is a relative form of the bounded construction which applies simultaneously to all ordinary surfaces in Q1. Given two nonempty finite ordinary computads \(X,P\), a chosen vertex in each, and a finite degree bound \(h\), one can effectively embed both in a finite computad \(W\), identifying the chosen vertices. For every \(d\le h\), each surface fails somewhere in \(W\) in degree \(d\) exactly when it fails somewhere in \(P\) in degree \(d\). This tests the *whole* of \(W\), including boundaries using declarations from both inputs. For an empty \(X\) just take \(P\).

First complete \(X\) at its chosen vertex to a locally finite ordinary presentation \(T\) weakly equivalent to the point. Use the walking-equivalence attachments of round-1 Response 129. To keep multiple vertices, introduce each other vertex as the opposite endpoint of a fresh walking equivalence out of the chosen vertex. Thereafter at each old declaration of degree \(k\) find a reference cell at its already included *literal* boundary, using weak equivalence to the point and existence reflection at prescribed faces. Attach a fresh name for that cell by the \(k\)-fold suspended endpoint inclusion. The name has the declared attaching type. Each pushout preserves the weak equivalence and adds finitely many names in each degree. The reference search terminates by enumerating raw typing derivations. The point inclusion into \(T\) is a finite composite of pushouts of these walking inclusions (each walk can itself have infinitely many declarations). The fold back to the point exists as a raw substitution: inductively fill each folded boundary over the point by its arity comparison. [Walking attachments, effective reference search and finite truncations](../answered/semistrict-surface-conservativity-2026-11-24.md#researcher-response-129) · [Ordinary computadic expansion of the walk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30254)

Form \(V=P\amalg_* T\). The inclusion of \(P\) is a raw weak equivalence by the very same sequence of walking pushouts, now starting from \(P\). The raw fold \(V\to P\) obtained from the fold of \(T\) is a retraction and hence a weak equivalence too. For \(W\), keep all of \(X,P\) and the auxiliary declarations through \(h\). This is a subcomputad since the attaching terms of the original names use only original names. The retraction restricts to \(W\). A failure in \(P\) remains a failure in \(W\) by inclusion of its surface witness and retraction of any proposed raw witness. Conversely send an arbitrary surface witness at old faces in \(W\) to \(P\) by the fold. If \(P\) reflects at this degree, the folded faces admit a raw inhabitant. The raw weak equivalence \(V\to P\) reflects existence in the iterated hom at the prescribed original faces, giving a raw inhabitant in \(V\). In degree at most \(h\) its formation can only use declarations through \(h\), all of which are in \(W\). The object case uses the chosen vertex. As a consequence, for each fixed \(h\ge4\) the \(\Pi^0_2\)-complete bounded recognition problem for \(J\) remains complete among extensions of *any* prescribed finite \(X\), even with the promise that the first failure is \(h\) or \(h+1\): use this construction through \(h+1\) on the reduction of Response 37. [Adjacent first-failure reduction](#researcher-response-37)

For the exact tail, first adjoin a generating 2-scalar and a generating 3-scalar at the iterated identities of the chosen vertex of \(X\) (supply a vertex if needed). Apply the point completion \(T\) above to this one augmented context. For *every* \(h\ge\max(3,\dim X)\) take \(W_h=T_{\le h}\). Every old type through \(h\) has a raw inhabitant: use the point comparison in \(T\) and then its degree bound. For \(d>h\) with \(d\ge5\) use the generating 3-scalar and the block test; there are no \(d\)-generators. The remaining case \(h=3,d=4\) uses the 2-scalar diagonal and the same support argument. This proves the exact spectrum in one nested sequence of finite extensions of \(X\). Its union has raw inhabitants at every old type, since every such boundary occurs in a finite degree. The finite examples distinguish postponing a first failure from restoring all-dimensional conservativity.

In fact the hardness promise can specify the **entire spectrum**. Fix \(X\) and \(h\ge4\). It is \(\Pi^0_2\)-complete, under the promise that an extension has spectrum either \(\{h,h+1,\ldots\}\) or \(\{h+1,h+2,\ldots\}\), to recognize the latter. In the construction with the machine presentation \(P\), keep the auxiliary walk declarations through \(h\). At the shared vertex also attach an independent copy of the cap-\(h\) completion of the scalar example (start with just the vertex and the two scalars). Through \(h\) the same fold proof works, by taking both full walking extensions over \(P\). In higher degrees the resulting finite computad retracts onto the cap-\(h\) scalar example: send the entire other factor through the common point and fix the scalar example. Such a raw point substitution exists at every attached type by point lifting. Thus *all* its higher failures persist even if \(X\) had declarations above \(h\). The two lower spectra are those of Response 37; on the promise, recognizing the later tail is precisely reflection through \(h\).

**Validation.** Run `python3 -B tools/semistrict_surface_relative_extensions.py --agda-dir DIR` and `agda --safe -i src -i DIR DIR/RelativeExtensions.agda`. The checker computes the integer degrees of 560 named pair projections on octahedral collision spheres, retaining independently chosen representatives from cabled blocks before and after their exchange. It checks the inclusions and the fold at caps two through four on presentations with 18, 39 and 81 declarations. Safe Agda checks the middle pair of substitutions, including the original unit-padded attaching face and the retained binary multiplication. The split injection in every sphere degree and the assertion for arbitrary mixed boundaries use the proofs above.
